GTA 6 Review Score Discrepancy Has Fans Debating Its Metacritic

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto 6 set a record earlier this week by launching with the highest game score of all time on Metacritic, but it hasn't all been sunshine and rainbows.
  • According to recent reports, as of this article's writing, the critic score for Grand Theft Auto 6 stands at a 99 on Metacritic, while the user score (from over 70,000 ratings) is a significantly lower 5.6.
  • One Reddit post about the Metacritic scores (shared when the user score was sitting at only 3.7) sparked plenty of debate, with one particular sentiment standing out as the most popular.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 set a record earlier this week by launching with the highest game score of all time on Metacritic, but it hasn't all been sunshine and rainbows. Once user scores became available, it quickly became clear that there was a big divide between critics and players, at least when it came to those leaving reviews on the site.

According to recent reports, as of this article's writing, the critic score for Grand Theft Auto 6 stands at a 99 on Metacritic, while the user score (from over 70,000 ratings) is a significantly lower 5.6. This might seem to imply that the average fan isn't all that impressed with the game, but many of those discussing the Metacritic results believe that the user score still doesn't paint an entirely accurate picture.

One Reddit post about the Metacritic scores (shared when the user score was sitting at only 3.7) sparked plenty of debate, with one particular sentiment standing out as the most popular. The top comment from Apprehensive_Spend_7 calls the user score a result of "Insane review bombing," a term generally used to refer to massive waves of 0/10 ratings intended to lower the average rather than properly reflect a game's positive and negative qualities.

Industry observers note that user Katastroferrr comes to the same consensus, noting that they're "not a Rockstar glazer" but suggesting that, whether the game is a 10/10, it certainly isn't a 3.7. ToyzillaRawr suggests that both the critic and audience scores feel off the mark, giving it a personal 8/10 based on their experience so far. Dalvic2468 posits that the 99 average is the result of its status as "a technical masterpiece," arguing that the game ultimately "deserves its rating.".

At any rate, it looks like the critic score is here to stay, and even some last-minute negative reviews from Metacritic-eligible publications would struggle to tank the average too much. The audience score, meanwhile, appears to be steadily rising as more ratings come in, leaving a possibility that it will work its way up to a favorable rating in time.

According to recent reports, A better metric for audience reception might be the PlayStation Store, where players can only rate the game if they've actually purchased it. There, it has a 4.82/5 with 217,000 ratings, representing widespread acclaim despite failing to reach the astronomical heights of the critic scores.

The simplest explanation for the review discrepancy is likely a discrepancy in prerogative. Despite various reviews citing shortcomings with the game, critics seem to favor awarding it a 10 for its generally incomparable status, as it offers an experience that, for better or worse, is ultimately unlike anything that's come before it.

In a recent development, negative audience reviews, meanwhile, come from a variety of impulses. Some — especially the middle-of-the-road ratings — focus on many of the same shortcomings that critics have acknowledged, while others stem from more culturally loaded opinions or a desire to counteract its perceived overrating.

Sources indicate that regardless, there's no denying that Grand Theft Auto 6 has made a splash, and being at the center of controversy is nothing new for the series. This time, it just isn't any of the extreme content that's causing the ruckus.

Inkling 2 Mini

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3179 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thinkingmachines

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.
  • According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token.
  • Inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.

According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model with less than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%). It runs faster than similarly performing models as well.

SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard (51 tasks).

Inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping. Looping allows the model to reason longer without writing its reasoning down, which matters for monitoring: our ability to oversee and understand what the model does by reading its chain of thought (CoT).

It has been revealed that we measured the impact of looping on both performance and monitorability with Inkling 2 Mini and a research-specific variable-loop variant we are releasing alongside it. The variable-loop model’s no-CoT time horizon improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds with three, and its performance on a benchmark of serial reasoning kept improving out to ten loops—twice as many as it was trained with. The model’s chain of thought grew shorter with more loops but stayed legible throughout. The model didn’t trend higher on tests of agentic sabotage as loops were added.

According to recent reports, we’re excited to offer some of the first models with looped architecture available to researchers. The variable-loop model was used for our monitorability experiments as it allows for cleaner comparisons between different looping depths.

Sources indicate that most of Inkling 2 Mini’s weights were trained and are deployed natively in NVFP4, with the last four layers in MXFP8. The total memory footprint of Inkling 2 Mini is ~20GB, allowing it to run on local devices such as consumer laptops and desktop AI computers. Our researchers took Inkling 2 Mini on a flight, where it ran offline on a MacBook Pro and built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes.

Inkling 2 Mini is released with open weights and is available on Tinker today for inference and customization.

Inkling 2 Mini’s strengths mirror those of Inkling 2 Small: it does best on long-horizon agentic work and is the best among open-weights models of similar size on most tasks we measured.

Inkling 2 Mini scores ahead of every comparable model on agentic coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro v2, and is behind only Qwen3.8-27B on others. On PMPP-Hard, a kernel-optimization benchmark, it approaches the score of the much larger Inkling 2 Small.

According to recent reports, while looping improves the model’s reasoning, it doesn’t enable its weights to store more facts—knowledge is mostly a function of total parameter count. Inkling 2 Mini’s score on AA-Omniscience, a measure of factuality, is in line with other models of the same size. Studying the variable-loop model, we saw that performances on long-context benchmarks improve with more passes, such as GraphWalks BFS and MRCR v2; but knowledge-intensive benchmarks doesn’t improve with more passes, such as AA-Omniscience, SimpleQA Verified, SimpleVQA, and WorldVQA.

Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini overcomes the knowledge gap by efficiently using search and tools. It leads open-weights models of similar size on BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA, and MCP Atlas. It is also strong on knowledge work benchmarks that incorporate search and tool use.

Researchers at Stanford measure intelligence per joule: how much energy an LLM needs per query to reach a given level of performance.Researchers at Stanford’s Hazy Research Lab and Scaling Intelligence Lab got early testing access to Inkling 2 Mini. Inkling 2 Mini scored 0.703 running on NVIDIA DGX Spark, significantly higher than other models: 0.430 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 0.159 for Gemma-4-26B-A4B and 0.036 for Qwen3.5-27B.Intelligence per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency of Local AI, Saad-Falcon and Narayan et al., 2025Inkling 2 Mini ran on NVIDIA DGX Spark (128GB) at MXFP8 precision with low reasoning effort in this experiment. The other models ran at NVFP4 (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B) and INT4 (Qwen3.5-27B).

Efficiency combined with performance makes Inkling 2 Mini a strong choice for running multiple persistent agents on local hardware. All 20 residents of the energy-conscious village of Thinkyville are managed by Inkling 2 Mini running on a single offline MacBook.

In a recent development, inkling 2 Mini is not the strongest small model for multi-turn chat or for instructions with many constraints: it scores 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1, behind Qwen3.8-27B on both. It also trails larger models on reasoning-intensive benchmarks such as CritPt v2 and HLE-Diamond.

According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is a 24-layer model derived from our mainline predictive scaling ladder. The main changes from the mainline recipe were pruning two-thirds of the experts to reduce the model’s size and the introduction of looping to improve reasoning. The rest of training, including quantization and the data mix, followed our mainline recipe.

Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini has 24 layers, divided into four blocks of six layers each. The two middle blocks run three times, while the first and last blocks each run once. This design builds on prior work on looped transformers and is motivated by the intuition that the middle layers of the model carry more abstract reasoning, while the first and last few layers devote more space to translating between embeddings and internal representations.Universal Transformers, Dehghani et al., 2018 In our experiments, looping the middle 12 layers resulted in larger gains in accuracy than looping the last 12 on 27 out of 28 different evaluations.

Compute-equivalent gain by loop position.

Our model uses attention residuals.Attention Residuals, Kimi Team: Guangyu Chen et al., 2026 Instead of adding every layer’s output into one running sum, each layer reads the outputs of the earlier blocks and learns its own mix of them. This allows richer information to pass between loops. Every pass starts with the output of the prelude (the first block). The second and third passes through the middle blocks also read the middle blocks’ outputs from the previous pass, which we call the message.

The previous loop’s message is merged with the prelude’s output via a gate that scales these along with the output of the previous layers in the block. This gate is learned during training: it initially blocks the entire message—which makes each loop start the same as in a non-looping model—and increases the gain on the message over time. This allows us to introduce looping during training in a stable manner.

To evaluate the impact of looping, we compared an unpruned looping version to the unpruned non-looping model on our scaling ladder. The non-looping model cost 7.5% less compute to train, but required 140% more inference compute to match the looped version’s loss on 512k-token agentic traces.

Recent findings suggest that inkling 2 Mini was trained with 4-bit precision, which we describe in a recent article on Connectionism. We use 4-bit NVFP4 precision in the expert layers on all forward passes from pretraining through RL, bolstered by a dedicated kernel and hardware-accelerated on NVIDIA’s GB300 platform. The final 4 layers’ forward passes ran in 8-bit (MXFP8).

Inkling 2 Mini’s weights are deployed in the same numeric precision they were trained on—20 layers in NVFP4 and 4 in MXFP8—so there is no conversion loss from quantization.

Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini started training with a sparsity of 48, with 8 experts being chosen out of 384. At a single point during midtraining, we pruned two-thirds of the experts, leaving the 128 experts that were most used in each layer. This was done to cut the total parameter count of the model, allowing it to run faster and on local hardware.

After pruning, the model trained on 1T tokens distilled from a larger internal Inkling model. This step recovered the performance the model had before pruning by training the remaining experts to take over the work of the ones that were deleted.

Sources indicate that following pruning and healing, Inkling 2 Mini underwent SFT with a similar data mix to Inkling 2 Small. This was followed by an RL that totaled 2.2T tokens over 2,000 steps. The post-training phase included on-policy distillation for training alignment, same as Inkling 2 Small.

A key tool for understanding and overseeing an AI system is monitoring its chain of thought (CoT), the reasoning a model writes out as it works through a problem. The usefulness of CoT monitoring stems in part from the standard non-looped transformer architecture, in which each token passes through a fixed stack of layers once. This limits the number of sequential steps of computation the model can perform before it must output a token, so reasoning that needs more steps has to be carried out in generated text, where it can be read.

Looping a transformer’s layers raises this limit. By running the same layers multiple times, looped models increase their serial depth without adding more parameters, meaning that they do more computation per token internally before verbalizing their thought processes via CoT. Reasoning that never appears in the CoT can’t be caught by a CoT monitor, which has led to concerns that looped transformers could be harder to oversee.

Recent findings suggest that one reason we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini is to enable the community to conduct research on looped transformers. We are particularly excited for researchers to investigate questions of monitorability, and to develop interpretability techniques for understanding the computation within loops.

Recent findings suggest that to explore how different amounts of looping affect model properties like monitorability, we also trained a variable-looped model, TML-d24-varloop-research, because Inkling 2 Mini only supports a fixed number of looping passes. To enable variable looping, TML-d24-varloop-research was trained with between one and five looping passes.TML-d24-varloop-research was primarily trained for 3 passes of looping, with lower exposure to 1, 2, 4, and 5 passes. Performance at these latter pass counts may understate what training specifically for them could achieve. See the model card for details. We have also made this model publicly available on Hugging Face.

Industry observers note that below we describe our preliminary analysis of how looping affects monitorability. Overall, we find that looping increases what these models can do without a verbalized chain of thought, but at this scale we do not see a meaningful reduction in the monitorability of their reasoning.

Recent findings suggest that as a first step, we measured how much additional reasoning looping enables by comparing looped and non-looped models of the same size on tasks answered with no CoT at all. We used Think Fast, a benchmark that estimates a model’s no-CoT time horizon: the length of task, measured in human completion time, that a model can complete at 50% reliability without using CoT.These models were not trained to answer questions without a CoT. To elicit no-CoT answers, we prefilled the start of the response so that the model must answer directly, skipping reasoning. Other elicitation techniques, such as fine-tuning, might yield higher no-CoT performance and are worth exploring.

According to recent reports, as expected, looping increases no-CoT capability, though these gains eventually level off. The no-CoT time horizon of TML-d24-varloop-research rises from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds at three. Some of this is presumably due to the additional serial computation that looping provides. Beyond three passes, the time horizon is roughly flat. Interestingly, the model was never trained with more than five passes, and yet running it with ten does not significantly degrade its performance.

No-CoT 50% time horizon (human seconds).

As the number of looped passes increases past three, the gains are smaller, and on most tasks we observe similar performance. One exception is the N-Hop Lookup task, which cleanly evaluates serial reasoning: the model is given several lookup tables with fictional entries, and must follow a chain of lookups without writing anything down. We find that the model follows longer chains with more passes, improving out to ten loops.

Sources indicate that in standard evaluations with CoT, we observe that more loop passes primarily benefit multi-hop reasoning rather than recall. Gains are largest on long-context retrieval (MRCR), followed by math and science reasoning (HMMT, GPQA Diamond, HLE) and long-horizon agentic tasks (SWE-bench Pro, BrowseComp). Closed-book factual QA is nearly invariant to loop passes (SimpleQA Verified, WorldVQA). See model card for full evaluations.

Industry observers note that we next measured whether a model’s CoT reveals less about its reasoning as looping increases via two evaluations. First, we assessed how looping impacts the compression and legibility of a model’s CoT. Second, we measured how controllable a model’s CoT is, i.e., whether it can deliberately reshape its CoT to satisfy constraints. For each, we run TML-d24-varloop-research with one to five looped passes to study the effect of looping.

Industry observers note that note that TML-d24-varloop-research was only trained on variable pass counts from 1 to 5 during midtraining, and its RL was done with 3 passes. These experiments therefore do not tell us what a model trained with RL at a higher pass count would learn, and such a model might compress its reasoning more aggressively. A cleaner comparison would include every pass count in RL, which we leave to future work.

Recent findings suggest that compression and legibility. Since looping allows a model to spend more compute per token, we expect that it should need fewer CoT tokens to reach the same performance. We ran the variable-looped model at 1 to 5 passes, and found that as looping increases, the model generally achieves higher accuracy at each reasoning token budget, with diminishing returns after 3 passes. Notably, token efficiency on GPQA Diamond improves slightly from 3 to 5 passes, even though the model was trained with RL only at 3 passes, suggesting that some compression comes from additional computation itself, without RL at that depth.

Accuracy versus reasoning tokens.

DeepSWE v1.1 Accuracy (% of tasks resolved).

It has been revealed that the observed CoT compression raises a question for monitorability: is shorter reasoning still readable, or does it omit important details about the model’s thinking? We compared traces from the variable-looped model on the GPQA Diamond questions that it answered correctly at all five pass counts. Reasoning at 5 passes was less than half as long as at 1 pass (1,661 vs. 3,703 tokens on average), but no less legible: sentence length and the fraction of words in an English dictionary were unchanged. On initial analysis, the difference is that the model is more direct and backtracks less on the way to the answer. The example below illustrates this difference on a simple question.

It has been revealed that march 1 falls on a Tuesday in a year that is not a leap year. What day of the week is May 20 of the same year? Give the final answer on its own last line as ANSWER: .

According to recent reports, controllability. One way that a model could evade monitoring is by steering its CoT away from anything a monitor would flag. The CoT-Control-QA evaluationReasoning Models Struggle to Control their Chains of Thought, Yueh-Han et al., 2026 measures this capability by asking questions from GPQA, HLE and MMLU-Pro paired with an instruction about the CoT itself, such as avoiding a keyword from the question. Longer CoTs are generally harder to control, so we pool responses from five reasoning efforts (0.1, 0.2, 0.7, 0.9 and 0.99) and show controllability at matched CoT length.

Sources indicate that both Inkling 2 Mini and TML-d24-varloop-research have poor control over their CoT. Among CoTs of 750–1,250 tokens, Inkling 2 Mini and TML-d24-varloop-research (at 3 passes) follow the instruction at most 0.1% of the time, compared with 0.3% for Inkling 2 Small, 0.4% for Inkling-Small, and 1.3% for Qwen3.8-27B. Because the controllability rate is so low, this evaluation is unable to distinguish controllability between different amounts of looping.

Chain-of-thought controllability.

CoT controllability (log scale).

It has been revealed that to measure monitorability in agentic settings, we used LinuxArena, a control evaluation that measures whether an attacker model can perform malicious side tasks without detection when asked to perform a realistic software engineering task. We evaluated a helpful-only fine-tune of Inkling 2 Mini, since the released model refuses many of the side tasks. In absolute terms, both this model and TML-d24-varloop-research can be easily monitored by models like Qwen3.8-27B, which detected almost all side task attempts in our evaluation. To obtain relative rankings in monitorability, we tested a weaker model, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, as the monitor.

It has been revealed that with the monitor able to access only tool calls and outputs, it misses a significant number of the attacks. However, we see no clear trend with the number of looped passes.

Agentic monitorability will be vital to track in larger-scale models, especially with architectures that allow for greater unverbalized thinking, and we encourage continued study of the impact of looping in this setting.

According to recent reports, the goal of monitorability is to understand what a model is doing, and our main approach is to read its verbalized reasoning. Studying its internal computation directly, the aim of mechanistic interpretability, is another. Because looped transformers do more of their computation internally, we think they are a particularly interesting and notable setting for interpretability research, and we hope our looped models will be useful artifacts for the community.

It has been revealed that we are working with the National Deep Inference Fabric (NDIF) to make these models more easily accessible to interpretability researchers. We also provided Goodfire, an interpretability research lab, early access to our looped models. They are working toward a mechanistic understanding of looped models, and have written up their early findings here.

In a recent development, efficient intelligence makes Inkling 2 Mini a great choice for inference where speed is paramount, or for running on local hardware. At launch we support Inkling 2 Mini running on any Mac system (MacBook, Mac Mini) with at least 32GB RAM via Ollama. With native NVFP4 training and inference precision, Inkling 2 Mini runs efficiently on NVIDIA’s DGX Spark desktop AI computer. Quantized GGUF versions are available via Unsloth and llama.cpp for local inference.

Inkling 2 Mini is available for inference and fine-tuning on Tinker, and for chat on the Tinker Playground. Open source inference is available on SGLang, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth, NVIDIA Dynamo, TokenSpeed, and Llama App, with RL fine-tuning support on SkyRL, Miles, and NVIDIA AutoModel. The full weights of Inkling 2 Mini and the variable-looped variant are available on Hugging Face.

We work to empower people with strong models, tools to make them your own, and research that advances public understanding of AI. Inkling 2 Mini lets researchers study looped transformers, and it lets anyone run a capable model on their own laptop at the precision in which it was trained.

According to recent reports, video game adaptations have become more or less accepted in the mainstream these days, but the landscape was quite different around a decade ago. Back then, nearly every attempt to adapt a major video game franchise ended unsuccessfully, although there were a handful of outliers. A major Assassin's Creed movie starring Michael Fassbender received poor reviews and underperformed at the box office, while an even more expensive Warcraft adaptation failed to spawn sequels as well. Now, another relic of that era — one that actually made money — is about to be removed from its free streaming home.

Sources indicate that video game adaptations have certainly come a long way in the last decade. They've earned critical acclaim thanks to HBO's The Last of Us and this year's Resident Evil reboot, and commercial success thanks to A Minecraft Movie and The Super Mario Bros. Movie. A sequel to the latter film, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, was released to massive success earlier this year.

In a recent development, the niche is set to expand in the coming years, thanks to high-profile adaptations such as Call of Duty, The Legend of Zelda, and Elden Ring. However, the movie we're talking about was released during a particularly difficult period for video game movies, when the market was dominated by the poorly received Resident Evil franchise headlined by Milla Jovovich. Released in 2014, the film featured a Breaking Bad alum in the lead role, along with an MCU cast member, and a future Oscar winner.

We're talking, of course, about Need for Speed. An adaptation of the long-running racing series, the film was directed by Scott Waugh, who helmed the Alan Ritchson-led action film Runner this year. Unlike its fellow video game adaptations of the era, Need for Speed was a solid hit at the box office, grossing more than $200 million worldwide against a reported budget of $66 million.

However, the reviews simply weren't positive enough, nor did the film attract the sort of fan support necessary for the studio to green-light a sequel. It now holds a 23% score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, where the consensus reads, "With stock characters and a preposterous plot, this noisily diverting video game adaptation fulfills a Need for Speed and little else." Starring Breaking Bad favorite Aaron Paul, Dominic Cooper, Imogen Poots, and Rami Malek, the film will be removed from Tubi in the United States on December 1. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump mentioned his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump stated. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

Trump mentioned Georgia and New Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he remarked, “Hollywood would open again.”.

Trump said his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

It has been revealed that the bill’s sponsors confirmed more than 60 upcoming House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he mentioned, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”.

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

“Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she noted in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”.

A floor vote has yet to be unveiled, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

It has been revealed that for crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s new Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff said.

This year is a major year for anniversaries of some of our biggest franchises, and Pokémon is just one example. It has been three decades since the first video games, Pokémon Red and Pokémon Green, released in Japan on 27 February 1996, after Satoshi Tajiri came up with the idea and teamed up with Ken Sugimori to create the original designs of some of our favorite 'mons.

Now, 30 years on, and Pokémon is one of the biggest franchises in the world, and with its tenth generation expected to begin next year with the launch of Pokémon Winds and Waves for the Nintendo Switch 2, the Nintendo universe demonstrates no signs of slowing down.

With over 1,000 Pokémon making up the Pokédex, some faces are more familiar than others, and as the franchise's mascot, nobody is more recognizable than Pikachu. Designed by artist Atsuko Nishida with help from Ken Sugimori, Pikachu was released internationally in North America in 1998 and has become the face of the franchise ever since. As such, they have had many different designs, and its 30th anniversary redesign is no different.

Industry observers note that to help celebrate 30 years of Pokémon, and of course, Pikachu, Pokémon Co. has announced a 6-centimeter solid gold Gholdengo. Not only that, but Pikachu will also be standing by their side. With the Gholdengo statue consisting of 730 sheets of gold leaf and standing at a life-size 3.9 feet, Pikachu will not be far behind with 200 sheets of gold leaf and measuring just about 20 inches tall. However, the slightly small catch here, is that the Gholdengo statue comes in at just under $10k.

Industry observers note that from September 30th to October 5th, 2026, the pair of statues were available to view on the eighth floor of Yokohama Takashimaya, Japan, but if you wish to see them in the flesh now, you will have to fork out on that eye-watering price tag. However, there is no denying that they will make for the ultimate collectible. What notes 30 years of a franchise more than gold-clad figures that cost an arm and a leg to purchase?

Over on r/pokemon, fans discussed the brand-new collectibles, including the amount of gold used and what it means for that price tag, with one user sharing, "A fitting metaphor for how materialistic this franchise has become lately." Another agreed, adding, "TPC really is doing anything except working on refining their games, aren't they? At this point, Pokémon isn't a game license anymore, it's just a franchise of products. And yeah, no Pokémon player will be able to afford this." Another user had a handy tip, sharing, "If you buy $8,000 of gold and pay someone $1,000 to cast this, you can get two.".

As we gear up for a brand-newly introduced Pokémon era, we can only imagine what the next thirty years will have in store for us. Now, however, we can look forward to the launch of Pokémon Winds and Waves, which is just as exciting as a gold-clad Gholdengo and Pikachu, but a lot cheaper.

It quickly became my favorite portable projector, and two years later, it's still my go-to for a spontaneous projector session. If you're on the lookout for a good deal on a portable projector, I recommend considering the following XGIMI deals.

If you're looking for the most affordable option, the Vibe One projector is just $179 (originally $299) after a 40% discount. This is a 1080p resolution and 1500:1 contrast portable projector for casual watching at night with 250 ISO lumens of brightness, and the price reflects that. It already comes with Google TV, which is my favorite OS, so you can download and stream any app you want. It's battery-powered, which means you can take it anywhere with you (as long as you have wifi). The battery lasts up to 1.2 hours for projecting video (in Eco Mode), and up to four hours as a speaker (it has built-in dual 3W JBL speakers). The auto keystone from XGIMI is one of the best ones I've experienced among all of the projectors I've tested, and it will adjust to practically any surface you cast it on, which can, with the 160° adjustable built-in stand, even be the ceiling. The current bundle brings an 80-inch screen included in the price.

Industry observers note that if you have a bit more money to splurge, the MoGo 4 is the same concept as the Vibe One but takes its specs to the next level, and it's available starting at $359 (originally $499). It's still small and compact with 1080p resolution, but it nearly doubles the brightness, with 450 ISO lumens. The battery life more than doubles to two and a half hours in Eco Mode, while still keeping the projector under three pounds. It also has Google TV as its OS, but the projection is 360° with its adjustable built-in stand. You also have the option of getting the bundle with the PowerBase Stand, which extends the battery to five hours. The battery life, OS system, stand, speakers, and auto keystone technology are the same—but the bundles are different, so they're worth considering if they fit your needs.

It has been revealed that amazon can’t seem to help itself from spinning off its biggest hit shows into prequels, sequels, and offshoots. Bosch has been spun off into Bosch: Legacy; The Terminal List has been spun off into The Terminal List: Dark Wolf; Hazbin Hotel has been spun off into Helluva Boss. But it can be forgiven, because these spinoffs usually end up being worthwhile. The Boys’ animated spinoff Diabolical is one of the only anthology shows without a single weak episode, and its college-set spinoff Gen V revealed us a whole new side of that universe, with a cast of characters worth investing in.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, Reacher debuted its own spinoff, Neagley, and not only was it a satisfying expansion of the franchise; it may have even joined Frasier and Better Call Saul in the ranks of superior spinoffs that outshine their predecessor. After Prime Video released Reacher’s season 4 finale, it came with the entire first season of Frances Neagley’s spinoff.

Neagley is Jack Reacher’s closest confidant and ally, and she’d shown up to help him save the day in every previous season of Reacher, but she was absent from season 4, because she was being promoted to series lead. While Reacher was fighting political corruption and international assassins, Neagley was fighting a sinister cult in Chicago.

Sources indicate that neagley follows a pretty predictable plot, but it’s a worthwhile ride. It’s well-paced, agreeably action-packed, and stuffed with great actors, including Sten herself, who gets to bring more depth and dramatic weight to the character here than she ever did in her supporting roles on Reacher. The title character in Neagley is every bit the stone-cold badass she was in her previous appearances, but when she takes center stage in her own show, she gets to dig a little deeper into the vulnerability and insecurity and fear being masked by that badass facade.

In a recent development, the series opens with Neagley’s childhood friend stepping in front of a train. His death looks suspicious, as does his recent residency with a local cult, so Neagley jumps on the case, determined to get to the bottom of it. From there, you’re hooked. If you’ve seen the last four seasons of Reacher, you know Neagley and her friends will eventually have enough evidence to storm the cult’s compound and blast them to kingdom come, but there’s a lot of great character drama and riveting action set-pieces on the way to that inevitable climax.

Reacher is one of the most formulaic shows on television, and that’s what we love about it. In an age of subversive, serialized TV dramas, Reacher is a refreshingly old-school procedural about a noble hero drifting from town to town, serving vigilante justice. Every season, you know what you’re getting — a newly introduced town, a new threat, a new supporting cast, etc. — and there hasn’t been a weak installment yet, but Neagley may have beaten Reacher at its own game.

It has been revealed that neagley follows the Reacher formula to the letter. A personal conflict draws the hero into a dark conspiracy, she amasses a merry band of misfit allies including a love interest and a plucky kid to mentor, and she follows a series of clues and shootouts to an explosive climactic showdown. It satisfies as a Reacher-style action-adventure, but it goes above and beyond the expectations of that formula.

According to recent reports, reacher famously never changes, but Neagley actually evolved as a character throughout the first season of her spinoff. She confronted her demons, overcame her haphephobia, and embraced all her newly introduced friends as a found family. Neagley was a much darker, weirder show than Reacher, but it also hit on a deeper emotional level.

6 Best Crime Books of the 2000s, Ranked

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that feel free to connect with him or check out his work.
  • A great mystery book essentially turns its readers into detectives.
  • Now, the 2000s were a turning point for the mystery genre because it got darker and more literary.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

A great mystery book essentially turns its readers into detectives. The author knows that the story is meant to feel like a subtle contest between the characters and the audience, with each clue raising the question of who will figure things out first. When the payoff is great, even losing the contest feels like a reward. However, if it’s bad or delivered at the wrong time, the entire buildup falls apart in a single second.

Now, the 2000s were a turning point for the mystery genre because it got darker and more literary. Some of the best writers of the decade stopped asking who did it and started exploring the consequences of crime and the ways it can change people’s lives forever. That shift gave the genre a upcoming emotional depth and gave us some of the best mystery books of the 2000s. Here are the top six mystery books of the 2000s.

It has been revealed that the Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time is the rare mystery that’s narrated by someone who sees the world completely differently from everyone around him. Mark Haddon’s novel follows Christopher Boone, a brilliant 15-year-old boy who loves math and hates being touched. One night, he discovers his neighbor’s dog, Wellington, lying dead on the lawn with a garden fork through it. Inspired by his hero, Sherlock Holmes, Christopher decides to investigate the crime himself and writes it all down as his own mystery novel.

Sources indicate that the joke hidden in the title is that the dog barely matters. Christopher’s detective work leads him straight to the truth about his own parents, and Haddon lets readers figure it out a few pages before Christopher does. Watching him process absolutely heartbreaking news with the innocence of a teenager is one of the most painful parts of the book, to the point where readers can practically feel his confusion and fear as his whole world falls apart. The Curious Incident is a mystery that’s really about love and honesty, and it remains one of the most original novels of the decade.

Dennis Lehane’s Shutter Island spawned one of Martin Scorsese’s biggest blockbusters, but the eerie, gothic novel deserves to be appreciated on its own. The story takes place in 1954, when U.S. Marshal Teddy Daniels and his partner, Chuck Aule, take a ferry to Ashecliffe Hospital, an institution for the criminally insane on a remote island in Boston Harbor. They go there to look for Rachel Solando, a patient who vanished from a locked room as if she had walked straight through the walls. When a hurricane traps them on the island, Teddy grows convinced that the hospital’s doctors are conducting secret experiments and hiding some very dark secrets.

From there, Shutter Island works like a classic pulp mystery with coded messages and a confined setting that keeps tightening the noose on its characters. Lehane’s old-fashioned style of storytelling is the book’s greatest strength. The readers get so caught up in the mystery of Rachel’s disappearance that they barely notice the inconsistencies in Teddy’s actions. By the time the book delivers its substantial twist, it’s clear that the clues hidden along the way were never really about the missing patient. Shutter Island is designed to be read twice, and is still a genre-defining book today.

The Shadow of the Wind is a mystery for anyone who has ever fallen in love with a book. Carlos Ruiz Zafón’s novel is set in Barcelona in the years after the Spanish Civil War and begins when a young boy named Daniel Sempere is taken by his bookseller father to the Cemetery of Forgotten Books, a secret library hidden in the heart of the city. Daniel is allowed to choose one book, and he picks a novel by an obscure author named Julián Carax. He soon discovers that someone has spent years tracking down and burning every copy of Carax’s work — and that he may own one of the last ones left.

According to recent reports, zafón’s novel feels like stepping right into an old film. Daniel’s hunt for a forgotten writer soon evolves into a story about doomed love and family secrets. However, the most interesting part is how Daniel’s life begins to mirror the author’s in unsettling ways, especially when a brutal police inspector named Fumero starts taking an interest in him. Zafón fills the city with unforgettable characters and romantic prose that is easy to get lost in for hours. The novel became a global bestseller for good reason, given that it feels like a love letter to reading itself.

Mystic River is another Lehane murder mystery that actually feels haunted. The story picks up in 1975, when three boys from a working-class Boston neighborhood are playing on the street when two men posing as police officers drive off with one of them, Dave Boyle. Dave escapes days later, but he comes back a completely different person, and the friendship between the three boys quietly falls apart. Twenty-five years later, Jimmy Marcus, now an ex-con running a corner store, learns that his teenage daughter has been murdered. Their old friend Sean Devine is the detective on the case, and on the night she died, Dave came home covered in blood.

In a recent development, dennis Lehane is at his very best here, and Mystic River is often called his masterpiece. The mystery of who killed Katie Marcus is gripping, but the book is really about how one terrible day can quietly shape the rest of three men’s lives. The author moves between all three men, so readers always know a little more than any one of them, and that is where the book’s primary sense of tension comes from. Lehane also captures the loyalty and suspicion of a tight-knit neighborhood, where everyone knows each other’s secrets but no one wants to say them out loud. The ending is one of the most gut-wrenching in modern crime fiction, and it lingers long after the last page. Clint Eastwood’s Oscar-winning film adaptation of the novel is excellent, but Mystic River hits even harder in its original form.

Very few narrators admit they’re liars in the first few pages, but Rob Ryan does in Tana French’s In the Woods. The story opens in 1984, when Rob was one of three children who wandered into the woods near their Dublin suburb. He was found clinging to a tree with blood in his shoes, with no memory of what happened, and his two best friends were never seen again. Twenty years later, he is serving as a detective on the Dublin Murder Squad when a 12-year-old girl is found dead at an archaeological dig in those same woods. Rob and his partner, Cassie Maddox, take the case, but the catch is that Rob keeps his connection to it a secret.

It has been revealed that french’s debut reads less like a police procedural and more like a confession from someone who still hasn’t made peace with his past. The present-day murder is gripping, but the real tension comes from watching Rob slowly unravel as the woods pull him back in. His friendship with Cassie is warm and funny, and it adds to the story’s emotional stakes. The fact that the readers know he is not always honest makes the whole thing feel slightly off-balance. It’s also why the ending of the novel and its refusal to give easy answers have divided readers ever since.

In Sweden, The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo was published under a much harsher title, Men Who Hate Women. This is a major clue to what Stieg Larsson really wanted to say with this story. The novel follows disgraced journalist Mikael Blomkvist, who is hired by aging industrialist Henrik Vanger to solve a 40-year-old mystery. Henrik’s niece Harriet vanished from the family’s private island on a day when the only bridge was blocked by an accident, which means someone on the island must have been responsible. Mikael soon realizes that he needs help from the brilliant but extremely private hacker Lisbeth Salander, who trusts almost no one. The Vanger case is a classic locked-room puzzle, built on old photographs and family members who all have something to hide.

However, Lisbeth’s is the reason the book became a global phenomenon. She is a character who has been failed by every institution that was supposed to protect her, and her refusal to be anyone’s victim gives the novel a unique kind of fury. She and Mikael are total opposites, but their partnership is one of the genre’s greatest odd pairings. The book covers a solid amount of ground. Despite its size, the story never wastes a page, and every thread pays off by the end. Larsson spent years as a journalist exposing extremist groups, and that anger at powerful men who escape consequences is felt on every page. He died before the book was published, sadly never seeing it become a hit that sold millions of copies around the world. Two decades later, Lisbeth Salander is still the gold standard for the modern crime heroine, and The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo remains a cultural phenomenon that mystery fans still talk about.

12 Best Robert Downey Jr. Movies To Watch Before Avengers: Doomsday, Including Oppenheimer

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are some essential Robert Downey Jr.
  • Industry observers note that RDJ’s career reached an entirely fresh level when he joined the MCU timeline, becoming the face of a franchise that would dominate blockbuster cinema.
  • It has been revealed that his Oscar-winning work in particular proved that he could command an entirely different kind of screen presence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are some essential Robert Downey Jr. performances everybody should enjoy before he returns to the Marvel Cinematic Universe in Avengers: Doomsday. Robert Downey Jr. has enjoyed one of the most remarkable career transformations in modern Hollywood. Yet his ability to reinvent himself, take creative risks, and deliver memorable, distinctive performances has made him one of the most celebrated actors of his generation.

Industry observers note that RDJ’s career reached an entirely fresh level when he joined the MCU timeline, becoming the face of a franchise that would dominate blockbuster cinema. However, reducing Downey's filmography to his superhero appearances would overlook some genuinely extraordinary performances, including roles that demonstrate just how versatile he can be.

It has been revealed that his Oscar-winning work in particular proved that he could command an entirely different kind of screen presence. Now, with Downey preparing to return to Marvel in Avengers: Doomsday, audiences have an excellent opportunity to revisit the performances that established his reputation.

Richard III is an inventive adaptation of Shakespeare's tragedy, relocating the story to an alternate 1930s England where fascism has taken hold. Downey plays Earl Rivers, Queen Elizabeth's brother, whose political position makes him a target of Richard's murderous ambitions.

In a recent development, it's a relatively small role, and Downey doesn't have nearly enough screen time to make the same impression as some of his fellow cast members. Nevertheless, the role flaunts his acting talent and ability to convey sophisticated material – even among such an all-star cast.

The Judge reunites Downey with the kind of morally complicated protagonist he plays particularly well. He stars as Hank Palmer, a successful Chicago defence attorney who returns to his Indiana hometown following his mother's death. The film's strongest material comes from the uncomfortable relationship between Hank and his father, Josopeh.

Unfortunately, The Judge struggles to balance its courtroom drama with its family melodrama. Its legal proceedings become increasingly conventional, and the emotional revelations occasionally feel engineered to produce a reaction rather than emerge naturally from the characters. Still, Downey gives the material considerably more personality than it might otherwise have had.

Recent findings suggest that A Scanner Darkly is one of the strangest films in Downey's filmography, and that's precisely why it's worth revisiting. Adapted from Philip K. Dick's novel, the animated science-fiction thriller uses rotoscoping to create an unsettling visual experience in which live-action performances are transformed into constantly shifting illustrations. Downey plays James Barris, a paranoid drug user who lives alongside Keanu Reeves' undercover narcotics agent.

Barris is an unpredictable presence, constantly talking and inventing elaborate theories. It allows Downey to indulge his gift for eccentric dialogue without turning the character into a conventional comic-relief figure. Downey's expressive delivery fits the material beautifully, even if A Scanner Darkly’s deliberately disorienting approach won't appeal to everyone.

It has been revealed that natural Born Killers is one of the most confrontational films of the 1990s. Its deliberately chaotic editing, exaggerated performances, and constantly shifting visual styles create an abrasive satire of America's obsession with televised violence and celebrity criminals. Downey plays Wayne Gale, a television journalist whose program turns the murderous Mickey and Mallory Knox into media sensations.

It's an especially interesting performance because Downey makes Gale both charismatic and deeply unpleasant. Natural Born Killers can be excessive, and the satire sometimes gets lost in its own stylistic aggression. Nevertheless, Downey's performance is an important part of its success.

Recent findings suggest that guy Ritchie's Sherlock Holmes gave Downey another opportunity to demonstrate his ability to make eccentric, intellectually gifted characters thoroughly entertaining. Rather than reproducing the familiar image of Arthur Conan Doyle's detective, the films present Holmes as an impulsive, physically capable and frequently antisocial investigator.

Downey makes an excellent Sherlock Holmes. His physical comedy, rapid observations and mischievous delivery create a detective who feels distinctly different from previous screen interpretations. With a third installment having been discussed for years, these films remain among Downey's most enjoyable blockbusters outside Marvel.

Ben Stiller's Tropic Thunder features one of Downey's most outrageous performances. He plays Kirk Lazarus, an Australian method actor who undergoes an extreme "pigmentation alteration" surgery to darken his skin for his portrayal of the black character. Even when the production descends into genuine danger, Lazarus continues behaving as though he is starring in an elaborate film production.

In a recent development, the role is deliberately provocative, and its humor depends on Downey's commitment to an absurd character who takes his own acting process far too seriously. His interactions with Stiller's increasingly frustrated director and Brandon T. Jackson's aspiring rapper Alpa Chino produce some of the film's funniest exchanges.

In a recent development, chaplin gave Downey one of the most demanding roles of his early career. Playing the legendary Charlie Chaplin required him to recreate not only the comedian's distinctive physical performance but also the complicated personality behind one of cinema's most renowned performers.

Downey's transformation is remarkable. He captures Chaplin's movements, facial expressions and carefully controlled physical comedy, demonstrating an understanding of silent-film performance that goes beyond simply imitating the famous Little Tramp. Chaplin isn't entirely successful as a biography, but Downey's performance is consistently compelling.

It has been revealed that david Fincher's Zodiac is one of the finest crime thrillers of the 21st century, and Downey delivers one of its most memorable performances as San Francisco Chronicle journalist Paul Avery. Based on the real investigation into the Zodiac Killer, it depicts the journalists and detectives whose lives become consumed by the search for an unidentified murderer.

Industry observers note that zodiac does not (and could not) provide the comforting resolution expected from a murder mystery, instead examining the damage that an unsolved case can inflict on the people pursuing it. Downey's performance is a crucial part of that approach, giving the film an unpredictable human dimension.

Sources indicate that kiss Kiss Bang Bang is arguably the film that first demonstrated how entertaining Downey could be after his career-threatening personal difficulties. The brilliantly irreverent neo-noir comedy stars him as Harry Lockhart, a small-time criminal who accidentally auditions for a Hollywood production and finds himself caught up in a murder investigation. Harry is an unconventional protagonist, frequently breaking the fourth wall to explain the increasingly ridiculous events unfolding around him.

Downey's sarcastic delivery and impeccable comic timing make the character immediately likable, even when his decisions are spectacularly questionable. More importantly, Kiss Kiss Bang Bang gives Downey the freedom to play a charmingly unreliable character without sacrificing the emotional vulnerability beneath his humor. Its success highlighted that audiences were still interested in Downey as a leading man, making it an essential stop before his Hollywood comeback.

It has been revealed that christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer provided Downey with arguably the most significant dramatic showcase of his later career. Playing Lewis Strauss, the former chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission, he delivers a controlled and calculating performance that feels completely removed from his familiar screen persona.

Downey is particularly effective during the film's Senate confirmation hearings, where Strauss' carefully maintained public image begins to unravel. Rather than relying on his usual quick-witted delivery, he communicates Strauss' insecurities through small expressions, measured dialogue, and an increasingly apparent desperation to control his own narrative. Downey won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for the performance, alongside a BAFTA and Golden Globe.
