💡 Key Takeaways
  • In perhaps the first instance where Magic: The Gathering caused a legitimate supercomputer to time out, exponential behavior strikes again as the bane of every computer scientistâs existence, prompting reflection: What is it about Magic: The Gathering that is so unique?
  • Recent findings suggest that I have been fascinated with Magic: The Gathering for years, not only as a remarkably fun and strategically deep game, but also as a mathematical and computational space.
  • It has been revealed that I began theorizing methods to improve AI play of Magic as early as 2024 but did not begin any implementation work on this until mid 2026; I first evaluated Forge and then decided that it was not feasible to get Forge up to a level of performance such that it could serve as an experimentation environment for RL on Magic itself, and thus decided to implement my own rules engine, Arcana.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In perhaps the first instance where Magic: The Gathering caused a legitimate supercomputer to time out, exponential behavior strikes again as the bane of every computer scientistâs existence, prompting reflection: What is it about Magic: The Gathering that is so unique? Why has it been so hard to achieve a true software implementation of the game?

Recent findings suggest that I have been fascinated with Magic: The Gathering for years, not only as a remarkably fun and strategically deep game, but also as a mathematical and computational space. The game is remarkably complex, even Turing complete, with intricate keywords and a daunting amount of mechanicsa, presenting an immense computational challenge for making the game run on a computer, let alone machine-playable. There are multiple existing software implementations of Magic; Arena is the most prevalent, developed by Wizards themselves, but there are numerous issues: the card catalog is notoriously incomplete, missing cards from the majority of the gameâs history; the matchmaking methodology, particularly for ranked play, is absolutely horrificb, and the performance of the game is quite poor, particularly when there is a lot on the stack. MTGO resolves the card catalog issue, but introduces issues of its own, including lack of adoption, a rather outdated and difficult to use interface, and so on. Meanwhile, Forge, an independent implementation, is promising at first glance â but the AI play is quite poorc, multiplayer is quite buggy and not truly supported, the interface is unintuitive, and the performance is still not ideal, even if improved over Arena.

It has been revealed that I began theorizing methods to improve AI play of Magic as early as 2024 but did not begin any implementation work on this until mid 2026; I first evaluated Forge and then decided that it was not feasible to get Forge up to a level of performance such that it could serve as an experimentation environment for RL on Magic itself, and thus decided to implement my own rules engine, Arcana. I figured that I could also design with multiplayer in mind from day one as a nice bonus and motivator.

In a recent development, one of the sources of my fascination with Magic, and, indeed, one of the reasons that a truly performant and complete software implementation of the game has yet to be achieved, is the nature of abilities in the game. Abilities in Magic can compound exponentially, and the amount of different possible interactions that can occur when any ability is triggered leads to a situation where although there may not be an unfeasible amount of state in principle, the amount of checks that are required to ensure that no further side effects must be put on the stack also grows exponentially, and as we all know, exponential behavior is an enemy of us mere mortal computer scientists. My fascination with the exponential behavior of Magic came back to bite me in an unexpected way.

According to recent reports, one of my favorite decks I ever devised was very simple in mechanicism and brutal in computational complexity. It revolves around a notorious card: Scute Swarm. To explain how this deck worked, we need a bit of background on the internals of Magic.

The core quantity of Magic: The Gathering is life; it can be thought of as the playerâs score, or an encapsulation of how well the player is doing. Each player begins with 20 life, and the primary way to win the game is to reduce the opponentâs life score to 0 (or below) before your own life score is reduced as such. There are different types of cards that can be used, and on any given turn, a player may use the resources granted to them by lands, the type of card that forms a basic currency in the game, to deploy whatever they wish within the gameâs limitations and rules.

According to recent reports, perhaps the most important type of card is a creature. These are equivalent to the prototypical card in most trading card games, like Pokemon; they can attack the opponent and defend from the opponentâs attacks. Scute Swarm is one example of a creature.

There are also tokens, which are special cards that are the result of an ability of a different card rather than a card that you play. One might use a card to earn a token, but one would not have a token in the deck that they build, and they would not ever have a token in their hand so to speak. The actual mechanics here are a bit complicated, but the significant picture is that tokens come into existence as a result of some ability and not from being in the playerâs hand or deck outright.

Scute Swarm is perhaps the most notorious example of a Magic card that exhibits exponential behavior. It has the ability, when a new land is deployed, to double the amount of copies of itself that exist. In practice, this is usually countered early, as Magic allows for many different waysd to avoid the exponential being realized (which, if substantially realized, will lead to victory for the person who played Scute Swarm practically invariably). If you combined this, I realized, with cards that produce life-gain whenever a new creature enters the battlefield, then one would have exponentially growing life. To make this even worse, one could play an artifact that doubles the amount of tokens that are created whenever any token is created, and throw in something to persistently double the amount of life gained. Seems like quite the loophole, eh?

For the arithmetic, the sixth land matters. Below six lands a Scute makes an ordinary 1/1 Insect. With six or more when the ability resolves, it makes a copy with the same landfall ability. Give each landâs triggers time to resolve before the next land comes down and every latest copy gets to help with the next batch.e.

In a recent development, suppose Soul Warden and Essence Warden are both in play. Each gives you one life for each fresh Scute. With a life-gain doubler thatâs four life per arrival, and with a token doubler each existing Scute makes two new ones. Hereâs what eight land drops would buy you under those assumptions.

This is totally egregious! Considering that a player begins with 20 life in Magic, and life gains are usually modest if present at all, a change of 3 orders of magnitude warrants that notoriety that Scute Swarm has. For comparison, I think (playing decks outside of this one) that, on paper cards, the highest life total I have achieved in a game is around 150.

The Scute curve is something we can work out on paper, but Arcana doesnât yet support scute swarm (deliberately, I might add). It was the purple curve that got me into trouble.

Now, who is this Liliana in the above plot?

Planeswalkers are, in a way, the heroes of Magic. They usually have multiple abilities, the most expensive of which (usually positioned at the bottom as the last one) we tend to call the âultimateâ â simply put, if you are playing against an opponent with a Planeswalker, youâd best ensure they donât trigger that ability. In some cases, the ultimate can create a special type of cardf called an emblem. Emblems are particularly concerning for you if your opponent has the opportunity to procure one, and particularly advantageous if you have the ability to use one, chiefly because they persist even if the Planeswalker is removed from play. An ability that an emblem provides will be in effect for the remainder of the game, typically leading to devastating and, importantly, compounding consequences for the opponent.

Sources indicate that liliana, the Last Hope is one such planeswalker. Her ultimate happens to create quite the dire situation not only for the opponent, but also for those who are interested in implementing Magic in software. When her ultimate ability resolves, the resulting emblem ensures that more and more zombie tokens are deployed onto the battlefield in a matter not too unlike that of Scute Swarm. Unfortunately for us as implementers, and for those who play against Liliana as losers, the amount of zombies that are deployed grows exponentially. What is unlike Scute Swarm is that clearing away the Zombies leaves the emblem intact and able to rebuild the army, whereas removing every Scute Swarm removes the source of its growth.

Industry observers note that letâs formalize what happens. At the beginning of each of your end steps (the last part of a playerâs turn), the emblem triggers. When that ability resolves, it counts the Zombies you control and creates that many more, plus two. With six Zombies already on the battlefield, you get eight upcoming ones, leaving fourteen.

Let ZnZ_n be the number of Zombies after nn resolutions of the emblemâs ability. Start with no Zombies (Z0=0Z_0=0) and one emblem, and suppose nothing else adds or removes Zombies or changes how many tokens are created. Each resolution then gives us:.

Sources indicate that zn+1=Znâalready there+(Zn+2)ânewly introduced arrivals=2Zn+2. Z_{n+1} =\underbrace{Z_n}_{\text{already there}} +\underbrace{(Z_n+2)}_{\text{new arrivals}} =2Z_n+2.

The first few populations are 0,2,6,14,30,62,â¦0,2,6,14,30,62,\ldots. After nn resolutions, that gives Zn=2n+1â2Z_n=2^{n+1}-2. Crucially, the army will always restart: even if every Zombie is destroyedg, the next resolution produces two more.

This forms Lilianaâs purple curve in the comparison above: 510 Zombies after eight resolutions. That plot counts growth events along the horizontal axis: one emblem resolution for Liliana, or one land entry for Scute Swarm.

Arcana implements that counting rule directly:.

Industry observers note that here, x counts the new arrivals, and the loop produces a separate CreateToken effect for every one of them. The engine then has to process all those arrivals, including the rules checks and any abilities they set off. As the army grows, so does the work required to resolve the emblemâs ability.

Recent findings suggest that letâs step back for a second. I was trying to decide which gaps in Arcanaâs rules to fix next. I had 64 Pioneer decksh and a list of 37 cards with known problems. There were 2,016 distinct pairs of decks. I played each pair twice, once with each deck going first, giving me 4,032 games in which to count how often those situations came up.

Industry observers note that in an effort somewhat analogous to fuzzing, I scheduled that entire 4,032-game lineup another 100 times. Each run used a different random seedi, and both players chose their actions at random. That meant 100Ã4,032=403,200100 \times 4{,}032 = 403{,}200 additional games to see whether I could trigger a panic, crash, or stall in the engine.

According to recent reports, all ~400,000 games are independent, with no intertwined dependencies between them. Thus, the work parallelizes nicely to HPC, and I typically run these games on a cluster rather than my own hardware. (This is especially important when I run larger trials and RL experiments using the engine, but still nice-to-have for purposes like this!) Unfortunately, when I did this on this occasion, nine jobs hit their two-hour limit. The random seed and the two decklists let me replay a single stalled game on my laptop and time its individual steps.

Recent findings suggest that in that game, one player activated Lilianaâs ultimate on turn 34. Once the army had grown into the thousands, one resolution of the emblem took 35 seconds on my laptop. That was a single engine step. Both players had let the ability resolve. Before either could make another decision, Arcana had to put every upcoming Zombie onto the battlefield and check what its arrival triggered.

Industry observers note that letâs take the first of those Zombies. A creature you control might have evolve, an ability that can give it a +1/+1 counter when a creature with greater power or greater toughness enters under your control. The engine has to find every creature that qualifies as followsj.

According to recent reports, this code is a walk of the battlefield. For each other permanent you control when one of your Zombies enters, effective_keywords computes its current characteristics to find out whether it has evolve. In this game, nothing had evolve, so the list came back empty. Then the next Zombie entered, and, most lamentably, the engine asked the same question all over again. Double the army and about twice as many Zombies enter, each scanning about twice as many objects. You can see where this is going: about four times as many checks are required to produce the same empty list.

It has been revealed that on turns 52, 54, and 56, I counted the Zombies at the start of the turn and timed the emblem when it resolved at the end. In one laptop replay those steps took 1.72, 7.78, and 35.15 seconds.

By turn 58, the opponent was at 31 life, facing 7,256 Zombies. At two damage apiece, sixteen unblocked Zombies would have been enough. The largest attack Arcana offered that turn used one creature.

Industry observers note that hereâs the view from the replay visualizer of the defending seat, just before the other player chose attackers. Donât miss the little badge in the corner of each Zombie pile! (The visualizer groups creatures with the same name, tapped state, power, and toughness onto one tile.).

According to recent reports, at a table, I can say âall the Zombies attack youâ and turn them sideways. In fact, with paper cards, thereâs essentially no chance that I, nor any reasonable human, own 7,000 printed copies of a 2/2 zombie token â so weâre probably using some other methodology, whether pencil and paper or an app on someoneâs phone that acts as a counter. In Arcana, unfortunately for us, we have to be quite precise about the state and transformations applied to it: the random player picks from a list, and each entry specifies the entire attack. On turn 44, each eligible Zombie could do nothing, could attack the player, or could attack one of the three opposing planeswalkers. Thus, we have a total of five choices per Zombie. Even with only five Zombies, there would be 55=3,1255^5 = 3{,}125 ways to declare attackers, and as you might guess, when there are thousands of zombiesâ¦ yeah, not good!

Arcana had a budget of 1,024 declarations. When the combinations exceeded that budget, the idea was to keep a few useful possibilities, encapsulating the decisions a reasonable player might make rather than providing all options. My justification for this was that if playing on paper, because as Iâve stated no one has 7,000 printed zombies, it would be incredibly pedantic to say â3,759 of my zombies are attacking you, and 3,497 are attacking planeswalker Xâ â no onekwould ever do this. Arcana reduces the options such that one could pass, send a single creature at any defender, or send everyone who could attack a particular defender at once. The pass was already in the list when this code ran. Look at the order of the two loops.

On turn 44, the arithmetic worked out pretty nicely. Of the 58 creatures on the board for the attacker, 56 could attack. Four defenders gave those creatures 56Ã4=22456 \times 4 = 224 ways to attack alone. Add the pass and the four ways to send every attacker at a singular target, and you get the 229 entries in the replay. Only one of those sent the whole army at the player, so odds are that the random player would miss it.

In a recent development, now, give that first loop 256 eligible attackers and the same four defenders. The single-creature attacks alone would take 1,024 slots, and passing has already taken one. That little return out exits the function, so crucially, the second loop never gets a turn.

According to recent reports, by turn 50, even a perfect player choosing from this list could send at most one creature. And what did our player actually do on turn 58? It sent one 2/2 Zombie after Oko, Thief of Crowns. The defending player stayed at 31 life. Then came the end step, and Lilianaâs emblem triggered again.

Recent findings suggest that arcana already knew how to call a draw when it saw the same settled position often enough; we had a system analogous to threefold repetition in chess, though ours was more for the convenience of the hardware Arcana runs on rather than any player computational or human. The random-play test itself also had a limit of 20,000 actions per game. Each time Lilianaâs army doubled, that check saw a position it had never previously seen. On turn 58 the replay got as far as action 2,325, passing priority to let the emblem resolve. Sixty seconds later, my poor laptop probe was still waiting for that one call to return, with plenty of actions left in the budget.

It has been revealed that recall that we had 64 decks; only four of them actually contained Liliana, the Last Hope. (Doesnât her name take a special irony at this point? I find it wonderful.) Indeed, as one might expect, all nine jobs that timed out had one of those four decks in the game they left unfinished. For the next run, then, I made the test harness count every permanent on both sides of the battlefield. With the limit set to 500, the check in the random-play test looks like the following.

Industry observers note that that explains the slightly odd-looking result from replaying another stalled game with the limit on. It stopped on turn 48 at 576 permanents, 0.16 seconds into the game! Why was this, you ask? An entire batch of tokens can arrive during one step. The harness sees the latest board as soon as that step finishes, records the turn and size under its own outcome, board_cap, and moves on to the next game. When I count wins, losses, and draws, I can still see exactly which games the experiment cut short.

Recent findings suggest that this got the experiment moving again, but there are two engine changes Iâd still like to measure on this replay. One is to work out which permanents have evolve once and reuse that answer for as long as the relevant characteristics stay the same. The other is to reserve room for the all-in attacks before filling the menu with singles. I think both are necessary potential directions; the first might buy Liliana a cheaper end step, while the second would give the attacking player a chance to end the game before she gets one.

In a way, this was inevitable, wasnât it? I had it coming. Saying I knew the trouble I was creating when I envisioned the Scute Swarm deck with its exponential synergies would be an understatement; in a way, I recall having this subtle feeling of foreboding when I had the idea and first put a concept together in Arena. I knew both in principle what would happen (âwhat number comes next in the sequence 2, 4, 8, __?â) and what I wanted to see happen in effect (âjust how much life can I gain?â). Years later, it seems the true meaning of this foreboding sensation has been revealed to me. Liliana has obliged me, at a somewhat greater expense.

It has been revealed that perhaps what I find most remarkable about Liliana, though, is how legible the instruction is on her emblem, regardless of where within that exponential growth you are. One of the chief criticisms of Magic as a game is that the instructions are often jargon heavy and difficult to interpret; indeed, one seldom sees a card (other than something like a basic land, of course) on Scryfall which hasnât accumulated multiple official rulings on interpretation over the years. Yet I think that with Liliana (who herself has accumulated such interpretations, indeed, so perhaps Iâm wrong) this is a nonissue. If you have 0 zombies you make 2, and if you have 7,256, you make 7,258 all the same. The amount of ink that the instructions need to describe the latter is exactly the same as how much describes the first, yet the latter can evidently be the cause of much more tumult. Thatâs some of the magic of Magic for me, in a way. I can hold a deck of 60 cards just like my Scute Swarm creation in my hand in an afternoon and years later, Iâm still discovering exactly what it is that Iâm holding.

Recent findings suggest that these are split between âevergreens,â which are the ones more familiar players like myself will know, and the rest; Magic introduces at least one upcoming keyword for every new set introduced, which can often be the source of great confusion. Luckily, the new ones are usually explained, and Scryfall is only a quick search away.â©ï¸.

It has never been proven (Arena is closed-source) but has been widely documented that, particularly at the highest levels of play, Arena almost uniformly ranks decks against other decks of similar archetypes. This infuriating situation defeats the variety in deckbuilding and strategization that makes the game fun. I quit playing Arena when I was ranked Mythic, and I lament the fact that I was not 18 yet and thus couldnât participate in the Pro Tour qualifier that I wouldâve otherwise been eligible for, as for this reason, I will never return to serious Arena play.â©ï¸.

Even worse, in fact, than that of Arena, which seems to be deterministically coded based on a few âstarter decksâ that do not rotate; at least Forgeâs can be played with any arbitrary deck!â©ï¸.

Instant removal is the obvious one, but if such is not available, countering the spell while it is on the stack is another option, as is exiling the card before the sixth land comes down.â©ï¸.

In a recent development, itâs actually a marker, not a card, but for our conversational purposes, itâs effectively a âcardâ as we would define it in colloquial English speech. Sorry, not sorry.â©ï¸.

Industry observers note that so, no, sorry, as much as I admire it as a card, Extinction will not save you. Exponentials always win.â©ï¸.

Recent findings suggest that these came from camilonunezâs collection of MTGTop8 tournament decks on Kaggle. Of the 800 distinct Pioneer decks I checked, Arcana had every card in the 60-card maindeck for 64 of them.â©ï¸.

According to recent reports, 2026 has been yet another busy year for Taylor Sheridan, despite the news that one of his most popular highlights from the last few years isn't returning before the end of the year. After Paramount released two full seasons of Landman in 2024 and 2025, there was hope that the show would return for its third season around the same time this year, but several production delays have led to the series being pushed back into 2027 at the earliest. Landman has taken the crown from Yellowstone as Sheridan's most popular show that's still on the air, but it has plenty of work to do if it's going to overtake Yellowstone in the long-run as his most-watched show ever. Viewership metrics for Season 3 when it releases next year will likely help shape the future of the series.

Earlier this year, Sheridan expanded the story of the Duttons with upcoming spin-off shows such as Marshals and Dutton Ranch, which changed his winning formula from years past. Previous Yellowstone offshoots like 1883 and 1923 turned the clock back with new characters, while Marshals and Dutton Ranch focus on characters like Kayce Dutton (played by Luke Grimes) and Rip Wheeler (played by Cole Hauser) who were first introduced in Yellowstone.

Recent findings suggest that now that Yellowstone is back in an era that fans are familiar with, it has left many asking if more crossovers are possible in the future, and there isn't a return anyone would like to see more than Kevin Costner's John Dutton. During an interview with USA Today to promote the second season of Marshals, Grimes was asked how he felt about a reunion, and his answer might shock you:.

“I think it would be cool [to have him come back]. I doubt that will happen at this point. I don’t know. If there was a flashback, I’d probably rather it be with Monica than John. I think that would be more poignant to the character. But we’ll see. There’s been no conversation, but we’ll see.”.

In a recent development, the show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

In a recent development, you are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

Industry observers note that kevin Costner and Taylor Sheridan didn't finish the final season of Yellowstone on great footing, which makes it unlikely that John Dutton ever returns in a future project, especially one produced or written by Sheridan. Around 2022 and 2023, Kevin Costner shifted his focus to his expansive Western passion project, Horizon: An American Saga, but after the first chapter bombed at the box office, the future of the series is in jeopardy. Two years after the first film was released in theaters, there is still no upgrade about when the second installment will be released, or if there are any plans for it to hit theaters or streaming.

They also cover Marvel and DC TV shows and movies, with a robust knowledge of comic books. Their TV reviews can be found on Rotten Tomatoes.

They also studied and participated in onstage and onscreen acting extensively from the ages of 7 to 18.

Aside from working at Screen Rant, Dani has worked as a freelance editor and writer over the past decade, often in a ghostwriting capacity.

Warning: This article includes SPOILERS for Percy Jackson & The Olympians season 3 and Rick Riordan's The Titan's Curse!

Disney+’s Percy Jackson season 3 jumps straight into the story, subtly setting up the most painful death in The Titan’s Curse from the start. The adaptation of Rick Riordan’s iconic book series is back, and it’s the best season yet. As critic El Kuiper mentioned in her review of Percy Jackson season 3 for ScreenRant, “Everything about Percy Jackson and the Olympians season 3 is more ambitious…” One of the biggest ways this reveals up is that this season is more gripping and wastes no time setting up the main story.

It has been revealed that past seasons have been criticized for taking the tension out of the story, and the writers seemed to have taken note. Like in the book, Annabeth is kidnapped almost immediately. However, the show introduces Atlas early instead of waiting, letting the characters and audience know the danger the Campers face. They cut the capture the flag game, which made sense in the Percy Jackson book but would’ve felt awkward in the TV show. Percy and Thalia get to use their water and lightning powers instead of having the moment cut off before anything happens.

On top of that, The Titan’s Curse includes a few major deaths. They don’t spoil this, unlike past seasons, which put significant book twists into the dialogue. There’s no telegraphing. That being said, Percy Jackson & the Olympians season 3 wastes no time foreshadowing Bianca di Angelo's death, the most tragic of all.

In chapter 13 of The Titan’s Curse, Bianca dies after she triggers Talos, the bronze automaton, in The Junkyard of the Gods by taking a Mythomagic figurine for Nico. She sacrifices herself so the rest of the quester group can continue. While the first two episodes only cover chapters 1 through 6, the Disney+ adaptation already set up Bianca’s death with three key hints, the most notable of which happens at the end of Percy Jackson season 3, episode 2.

Industry observers note that firstly, the Oracle chooses the questers instead of them deciding who’s going themselves, which is one of the least notable changes Percy Jackson season 3 makes to the book. The green mist spreads as the prophecy is read to pick out the 5 campers and Hunters who will go. To the unknowing eye, the order may seem completely random. After all, they pick people on lines like “The Bane of Olympus indicates the trail” and “Campers & Hunters combined prevail,” which aren’t focused on a single individual. However, the oracle picks Bianca di Angelo on the prophecy line about a quester being lost in the land without rain.

Read Along With Percy Jackson Season 3.

"My Rescue Operation Goes Very Wrong".

"And Old Dead Friend Comes To Visit".

Percy Jackson season 3’s credits once again hint at what’s to come in the rest of the season. About halfway through them, Talos, the giant bronze automaton, stomps his foot down on a Hunter. Because Bianca isn’t a Hunter yet, those who haven’t read the book won’t be able to put two and two together, though. The third hint is in the season trailer. When they say, “Victory will require sacrifice,” they cut together shots of the characters. They transition from Bianca in a Hunter’s jacket in the arid environment to Nico running through the forest crying.

Industry observers note that bianca di Angelo’s death is already very impactful in the book because she dies right as she’s figuring out who she is as a Hunter and who she is outside her caretaker role. She’s a prime example of an older sister who’s forced to be a parent instead of a child, and that finally starts to change right before she dies. However, the Percy Jackson & The Olympians TV show already sets it up as a more tragic death.

The show spent more time establishing the relationship between Bianca and Nico. They are much closer, which will make her sacrifice to get him a trinket more impactful. It will feel devastating that she will never get to see him again, and he will have to continue living without her. On top of that, Bianca didn’t choose to leave Nico in the TV show; the Oracle chose her.

Plus, Bianca has more of a personality onscreen. She has animated facial reactions, a wider emotional range, and strong opinions. She has connections to the other characters before she joins the Hunters, if she joins the Hunters. Obviously, we won’t know until more Percy Jackson episodes drop if that will happen. In the book, her existence and death felt to some like a plot device for Nico’s story. However, it’s already easier to get invested in her in the TV show, which will make her death feel more like a loss.

#85974. Latest Update: Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1166 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI.
  • It has been revealed that GTA 6 is absurdly large.
  • According to recent reports, alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI. You’ve preloaded the game on your console, you’ve taken the next month off work, and you’ve locked your phone in a Faraday cage and set it adrift at sea. You’re prepared to lock in, and you haven’t forgotten a thing…right? Well, just to make sure, here are the most vital tips to optimize your setup before you fire up the most anticipated game of the decade.

It has been revealed that GTA 6 is absurdly large. According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space. For high-end consoles like the PS5 Pro, that’s more than 10% of the available storage space, and close to half the space on the more budget-conscious Xbox Series S. There’s a good chance you’ll have to delete something to make room.

According to recent reports, alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it). External SSDs are probably the cheapest route, though you’ll want to make sure to use a high-speed USB cable to connect it. It’s even worth shopping around for alternate models of SSD. For example, at the time of writing, the popular 2TB WD_BLACK external drive was close to $200, but the exact same drive in pink was $132.

Industry observers note that you can also directly upgrade the storage of your console with expansion drives. The Xbox Series X|S supports proprietary expansion cards, while the PS5 and PS5 Pro can accept most M.2 internal SSDs. These will generally be faster, since they plug directly into the console via higher-speed connections than a drive hooked up via USB.

Sources indicate that let’s face it: Half the fun of any sandbox game is the weird, unique stuff that happens to only you. So you’re probably going to be hitting that “record recent gameplay” button more often than usual. While you’re cleaning up your storage space (or adding more), make sure to account for all the video clips you might want to save.

It has been revealed that file size of video clips depends on a lot of factors, but 4K recordings can generally take up to 0.5GB per minute of footage. You can cut that down by saving footage in 1080p instead, but either way you’ll want to leave a little extra space.

Game footage is also a pretty good place to look if you need to make room on your console and don’t want to delete any games. Be honest with yourself: You don’t need all those clips from Horizon Forbidden West you saved four years ago. Dive into the settings on your console and find the biggest media files you forgot you even had on there.

It has been revealed that according to Rockstar, GTA 6 will be targeting 30fps across consoles at launch, which is pretty low as modern AAA games go. Part of the reason for that is all the processing power going to rendering a complex environment, but it also means you won’t need a fancy high frame rate TV or monitor any time soon to get the most out of it. Still, it couldn’t hurt to check a few settings on your display.

First, make sure you’re using a higher refresh rate than 30Hz. While the game is targeting 30fps, it is technically capable of more, so if your console can keep up, you don’t want to accidentally bottleneck your frames. This setting will vary by device, so check the manual that came with your screen.

According to recent reports, also, make sure you have HDR enabled on your hardware. There’s a good chance this is already turned on for your TV, but sometimes other devices can switch display modes if they only support SDR. The game will help you calibrate your HDR settings for GTA 6 specifically when you launch it, but only if it detects HDR compatibility in the first place.

It has been revealed that if you’re planning to buy a console specifically for GTA 6, this might be one of those rare instances where a PS5 Pro really is worth the upgrade. According to Rockstar, certain features like ray-traced shadows will only be available on the Pro version of Sony’s console.

Industry observers note that more importantly, the PS5 Pro version supports PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), which upscales lower-resolution images to get better detail and higher frame rates out of the same hardware. Given that GTA 6 is already starting at a meager target of 30fps on most consoles, anything that can give your frame rate a boost is probably going to feel like a welcome improvement over the baseline.

Industry observers note that I’ll tell you a secret as someone who’s spent a lot of time testing different game controllers: Most of the time, you really don’t need an expensive “elite” controller. Most of the time. I don’t buy into the idea that a taller control stick is going to make you an esports athlete. It can be nice to have, but it’s not a game changer. What does matter is customizing your controls, especially for long gaming sessions.

It has been revealed that the DualSense Edge wireless controller is a favorite of mine, mainly because of the rear paddles and adjustable triggers. The former lets you map any button to a rear lever that you can access with your fingers underneath the controller, which can often ease some of the wrist strain of awkward button combos. And the adjustable triggers let you activate the buttons with less motion, again reducing repetitive stress.

According to recent reports, the Xbox Elite Series 2 controller has similar features for the Xbox, as well as custom caps for the D-pad. Both consoles’ versions of pro controllers are more expensive than the standard ones, but if you’re planning to game for many hours, it can be worth it to get a controller that’s more comfortable for you.

If you have an Xbox One, you don’t necessarily have to upgrade your console to play GTA 6, but you might want to take a look at your network. GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on day one, and you’ll be able to stream the game to an Xbox One console (as long as you purchase Cloud playtime as well or get some with your Game Pass subscription). This is the only way to play on a console older than the current generation, so if you don’t want to shell out for new hardware, this might be your best bet.

Xbox recommends a minimum of a 20Mbps connection to run cloud gaming, but more is obviously better. If you can connect your console to a wired Ethernet connection, that would be better and provide more stability. If you can’t connect a cable, then at least make sure you’re well within range of your wifi router, and try to limit any other bandwidth-hogging applications on the network while you’re playing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable customers to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow customers to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed owners to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”.

A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of Fresh Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta noted they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same concerns.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

According to recent reports, keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, mentioned that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

Update, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple mentioned:.

“We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for customers. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”.

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The tech giant added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

In a recent development, just curious. Why doesn't someone from Apple try out the app before approving it, rather than approving it and waiting until people complain? I know there are many thousands of apps on the App store. But given that Apple makes money off most of these apps, it could surely afford to hire a staff charged with reviewing submitted apps to ensure compliance with the App store's guidelines and requirements before making them available in the App store. What am I missing here?

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the tech giant said does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

It has been revealed that as for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

Recent findings suggest that apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The company stated that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

Revision, November 19, 4:00 p.m. ET: In response to Apple’s statement, TTP director Katie Paul reached out to 9to5Mac with the following comment:.

Sources indicate that apple’s statement on nudify apps sidesteps important issues and leaves out key context. The organization states it prohibits nudify apps but doesn’t address how its age rating system for apps contributes to the problem. TTP has shown how Apple relies on information provided by app developers to set age ratings—a self-reporting system that allows many nudify and pornographic apps to be misleadingly labeled a suitable for minors. Apple also continues to talk about removing nudify apps from the App Store, without mentioning that apps that are “removed” continue to be fully functional on people’s phones.

Industry observers note that there are many questions about Apple’s policy on nudify apps that the statement fails to address. Apple has adopted a limited definition of “nudify.” The organization defines nudify apps as capable of showing someone naked, not stripping them down to a bikini or lingerie. But the company also claims it bans “creepy” and “nonconsensual intimate imagery.” What if an app is used to depict a woman in a bikini without her consent? We have asked Apple to clarify that and have not heard back.

As for Apple’s comment that TTP relied on “older software,” that may refer to the fact that Apple rolled out new child safety features in the fall. Our research was conducted in summer 2026. But many of Apple’s new features pertain to parent-supervised accounts on Apple, which have to be set up by a parent. Apple relies entirely on parents to go out of their way to locate and enable these settings. This raises obvious questions about how many people actually do this.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • First seen in 1960, and then three years later as featured in the first animated Peanuts feature film, a now-iconic scene of Charlie Brown, Linus, and Lucy van Pelt lying on the grass and staring at the clouds won audiences over worldwide.
  • According to recent reports, it's hard to argue the effectiveness of the scene, too, given the lovable loser Charlie Brown's practically embarrassed, sheepish reaction to Linus' superior commentary.
  • Famously used as the intro scene for A Boy Named Charlie Brown, this iconic cloud watching Peanuts strip is quoted practically verbatim as this primary trio of kids unleashes their takes on the clouds flying overhead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

First seen in 1960, and then three years later as featured in the first animated Peanuts feature film, a now-iconic scene of Charlie Brown, Linus, and Lucy van Pelt lying on the grass and staring at the clouds won audiences over worldwide. In its essence, it's a great dichotomy of imaginative childhood wonder at shapes in the clouds, with Linus' comparisons being notably more highbrow and specific, while Charlie Brown's were, naturally, utterly humbled by this due to their sheer simplicity. Yet, creator Charles M. Schulz created this strip that's now commonly reported among his favorites such as in The Complete Peanuts volume 5: 1959 to 1960 via Win Wiacek.

According to recent reports, it's hard to argue the effectiveness of the scene, too, given the lovable loser Charlie Brown's practically embarrassed, sheepish reaction to Linus' superior commentary. But between the commentary of the three, all of their comments are fairly valid, with the August 14, 1960 comic strip quickly immortalized in both animated format and shortlisted by fans as a personal favorite of Schulz's. It says a pretty good basic summary of how each character views the world, while serving as an excellent scene to set the tone for A Boy Named Charlie Brown.

Famously used as the intro scene for A Boy Named Charlie Brown, this iconic cloud watching Peanuts strip is quoted practically verbatim as this primary trio of kids unleashes their takes on the clouds flying overhead. The outspoken Lucy gives a perfectly rational, simplistic approach, seeing them as big balls of cotton, while even prompting the other two to use their imagination to convey what they see. Linus gives an intensely specific set of descriptions like topographical maps, an American realist artist, and an oddly specific description of the Stoning of Stephen.

It's especially funny to watch the animated version as Charlie Brown repeatedly cranes his neck, clearly trying to spot what Linus sees in the clouds above, growing more distressed that he's just not seeing it.

In a recent development, then comes Charlie Brown's turn, as he's called on to say what he sees. He gives throwaway animal shapes like a ducky or a horsey, perfectly legitimate options for a child to give, but retracts them, perhaps believing he could have used his imagination more effectively. None of the kids laugh or are even phased beyond Charlie Brown himself, as the film moves to the opening credits sequence from then on.

It sets the tone well for what viewers can expect from the characters, and the comic strip clearly inspired other moments like 1975's Snoopy! The Musical, in which Charlie Brown is joined by an even larger group of friends who consistently talk over him with what they see in the clouds. It even has an identical ending, with everyone turning to a blushing Charlie Brown, who once again gives his throwaway animal shapes even after a song's worth of colorful descriptions. Perhaps more than anything else, this comic strip has continued to strengthen the perception of Charlie Brown as a character, and his particular struggles.

It has been revealed that the humility of Charlie Brown is a recurring element of Peanuts, both cementing his own vulnerability while keeping him grounded, affable, and unpretentious. His descriptions are those of the average kid, while people like Linus seem to offer up elevated perceptions of mundane reality. But it's also that same openness and self-awareness that show Charlie Brown's honesty as a character, willing to offer up what he sees while also being open to thinking a little further, or even just withdraw, in any of the adaptations of this particular Peanuts strip. It's awkward, and seeing him cut off every time in the musical number is rough, but it's completely relatable.

Recent findings suggest that part of being a kid is indulging one's imagination on all ends of the spectrum, as it helps their cognitive and social development. Charlie Brown might pull away, but at least he still described what he saw in the clouds, and it's clear that Schulz put a little bit of himself into that scene, namely, the shy, withdrawn side of the boy as he struggles to engage like the other kids. But it's also important that this side of childhood, vulnerability, enables anyone to be open to greater growth opportunities, whether cloud watching in Peanuts, or any number of other perfectly relatable, real-world scenarios.

#85967. Industry News: Windows has two settings that bring work back after restart, both off by default

📅 27 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (880 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Makeuseof ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Windows has two settings that bring work back after restart, both off by default

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Makeuseof

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I'd turned off every startup app, yet Windows could still reopen the apps I'd been using before a restart.
  • Together, they let Windows restore much of my interrupted workspace without making me open the same apps every time I start my PC.
  • Sources indicate that my restarts are never planned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I'd turned off every startup app, yet Windows could still reopen the apps I'd been using before a restart. I found this out after enabling a setting that was off by default on my PC. A second setting brought back my File Explorer windows too.

Together, they let Windows restore much of my interrupted workspace without making me open the same apps every time I start my PC.

Sources indicate that my restarts are never planned. A PC that's been slowing down forces some, a few low-memory crashes forced others, and updates add their own. Setting active hours only changes when an update restarts you, not what you come back to. Each time, the apps, tabs, and folder I was using are gone.

According to recent reports, the first setting is Automatically save my restartable apps and restart them when I sign back in. It does most of the work. You’ll find it in Settings -> Accounts -> Sign-in options, under Additional settings. It was off on my PC, so I had to toggle it on.

According to recent reports, it's different from startup apps in Task Manager. That only opens the same list on every boot, whether you used them or not. This setting reopens what you actually had open before the restart.

I turned it on, opened Notepad with two tabs and some unsaved text, plus Firefox, Word, Settings, and two File Explorer windows, and restarted. Notepad was back before the desktop finished loading, with both tabs and my text exactly where I'd been typing. Firefox, Word, and Settings followed.

Windows doesn’t reopen every app in its exact spot. Settings came back on its home page, not the Sign-in options page I’d been on. That's a small price to pay compared with opening everything manually; even Workspaces doesn't do that much.

In a recent development, this is what sold me. I keep the session restore setting off in Firefox, Chrome, and Brave, on purpose. I use Rewind to restore whatever I’m working on, and I switch between editing and writing a lot. If a browser reopened old tabs on its own, I’d have to clear them out before restoring the session I want, and the tabs would pile up.

I want a clean slate every time I open a browser. None of them is in my startup apps either, and if I open any of them by hand, I get one empty tab.

According to recent reports, after the restart, Firefox came back with the tabs restored the way I left them, even before my internet connection was back, with no error page. In my later tests with both settings on, Chrome and Brave did the same. The Windows setting was the only thing I'd changed, and it was the only reason those tabs returned.

In a recent development, to me, that's the right behavior for a restore feature. On a normal day, I get a fresh browser. When Windows restarts and interrupts me, I get my session back.

Sources indicate that file Explorer didn't come back with the first setting, so I turned to the second option: Restore previous folder windows at logon. To find it, open File Explorer, select the three-dot menu -> Options -> View tab. It was off on my PC, too. I switched the restartable apps setting off to test the folder option on its own. Then I opened Downloads, Videos, and Documents in three windows, arranged them with Windows 11 Snap Layouts.

It has been revealed that all three came back with the restart, in the same layout, each in the exact folder I’d been in. I didn't have to navigate through any folder paths again, and nothing else reopened. So this setting does one job, and it does it cleanly.

The two settings are separate on my PC. Microsoft’s release notes for Windows 11 22H2 and 23H2 say turning on the apps setting automatically switches on some File Explorer settings, and they describe a gradual rollout. On my 25H2 build, the folder box stayed unchecked after I turned the apps toggle on, and Explorer stayed closed until I ticked it myself. If you want both, switch on both.

Industry observers note that the fair complaint is that it doesn't bring everything back. With both settings on, I had nine apps open: Chrome with eight or nine tabs, Brave, Firefox, Word, Notepad, Paint, File Explorer, VLC, and CapCut with a file open.

Seven came back where I left them, including the browser tabs. VLC and CapCut never opened. I felt the CapCut exception because I do my edits there, so I still had to relaunch and find my files again.

These settings don’t guarantee that every app will return or resume exactly where it stopped. But I'll still take that every time. Without the settings, a restart leaves me with an empty desktop and nine apps to reopen from memory. With them, I open two apps manually.

If your PC regularly needs a restart, for whatever reason, enable both settings before the next one.

When the next revision asks for a restart, let it. Mine brought back the same apps as a routine restart. Whatever stays closed is your list to open by hand.

Zane Lowe shares Apple Music Radio audience numbers, recalls ‘crickets’ in the early days

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a new interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month.
  • Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.
  • In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue noted Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a new interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue noted Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:.

Industry observers note that we were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:.

When we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a big way on fresh and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:.

The really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are new or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe said “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very important to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a new logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe said he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:.

Recent findings suggest that we could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The issue of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:.

Industry observers note that well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a tech giant and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift….

#85965. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI
