📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer indicates it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big challenges.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • Sources indicate that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer indicates it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big challenges.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Sources indicate that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he notes he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his firm Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he notes can yield “small data” solutions to major concerns in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

According to recent reports, andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having stated that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Recent findings suggest that ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Industry observers note that having mentioned that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing manufacturer with millions of users.

According to recent reports, ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

Industry observers note that “In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and noted, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

In a recent development, over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing latest here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

Industry observers note that the data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one organization or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

Recent findings suggest that you often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from major data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

Recent findings suggest that when you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand latest model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

According to recent reports, ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having stated that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very swiftly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Recent findings suggest that could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Sources indicate that ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an crucial piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Sources indicate that ng: In AI, data cleaning is crucial, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention promptly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

In a recent development, for example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

In a recent development, to make these concerns more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a manufacturer approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

It has been revealed that one of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

In a recent development, ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift problem. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion consumers. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent latest neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s key for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Industry observers note that ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

Black Friday is usually a great time to grab a latest e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a significant discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

Recent findings suggest that if you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink promptly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

The X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

Recent findings suggest that these upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also notable to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing latest firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hockey romance reveals are rapidly becoming their own niche subgenre. First, Heated Rivalry took off, delivering a steamy look at the relationship between professional rivals. Then Off Campus took it to the collegiate level, exploring the unlikely dynamic between a hockey captain and a music student. These massively popular shows each highlight the sport in the midst of a love story, and the trend isn't stopping there. Icebreaker is poised to add to this list. Based on Hannah Grace's 2022 novel, the series is still a ways off, but it will offer a fresh twist on the concept while continuing the legacy of these popular series.

It has been revealed that netflix is bringing Grace's story to life, and the adaptation is already in production. Like Off Campus, Icebreaker will feature a college romance with hockey in the background, but one major element will set the story apart. In this case, the romance is between a hockey player and a competitive ice skater, giving the series even more reason to put them on the ice.

There is a lot to look forward to as Icebreaker joins the ranks of this genre. The book follows Anastasia "Stassie" Allen, a dedicated figure skater, and Nate Hawkins, the hockey team's captain, as their paths collide. Each has their own lofty ambitions, as Stassie hopes to go to the Olympics and Nate chases a spot in the NHL, and both are willing to put in the work. However, both of their goals are interrupted when a facilities mishap forces them to share space. With a heavy focus on body image challenges and found family, Icebreaker holds a lot of promise as this adaptation moves forward.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

It has been revealed that you do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

According to recent reports, you want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

According to recent reports, the intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

Industry observers note that you do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

Recent findings suggest that the series can expand the genre's focus by featuring two different ice sports. But for the characters, that isn't as compatible as it may seem. Though their mutual love for the ice seems like something they should bond over, they are positioned almost as rivals as they are forced to share the rink. However, that only increases the tension. In some ways, it's reminiscent of Heated Rivalry, which places the main characters on opposite teams. However, Icebreaker opens the doors to more variety as fans can also get insight into the world of competitive skating, which can only lead to more exciting scenes on the ice. Icebreaker has a lot of potential, and as the Netflix series nears, that will only become more obvious.

Industry observers note that while there's plenty of anticipation around Icebreaker, the series is still in its early days. Production has started, and, even more notably, Netflix announced the cast. Daisy Jelley and Connor Simos will play the lead roles, playing Stassie and Nate, respectively. Joining them are Gabriel Tierney, Auliʻi Cravalho, Peter Berry, Chaneil Kular, Devin Craig, Aidan Shaw, Paul Wesley, and Sara Canning. Behind the scenes, Jade Halley Bartlett will serve as the series' creator, and Amanda Lasher is set to be showrunner. Additionally, book fans should be excited that author Hannah Grace is expected to be involved in the production. Though Icebreaker has no release date announced, Netflix is actively working on the series, which means fans can expect more information soon.

It has been revealed that undoubtedly, now is the perfect time to adapt this book, especially as both Heated Rivalry and Off Campus are in production on their second seasons. Other streaming shows have proven there is widespread interest in the concept, but including figure skating adds variety to the growing genre. Grace's book, which kicks off her Maple Hill series, has spent years accumulating fans and offers ways to expand the series beyond this season. Already, Icebreaker has its own audience after the book has sold over 5 million copies, and that is even before impatient fans of Heated Rivalry and Off Campus flock to Netflix. Star Wars Rebels favorites Ezra Bridger, Hera Syndulla, and Garazeb Orrelios will have their work cut out for them.

Now, Ahsoka can begin training Sabine in earnest. Ahsoka left the Jedi Order during the Clone Wars. Sabine, meanwhile, is a proud Mandalorian warrior. Can she be both? Does she want to be? Sabine's confirmed new hairstyle suggests this will be the crux of her arc in Ahsoka season 2.

In a recent development, since her Star Wars Rebels debut, Sabine's haircut and color have highlighted her character, each style reflecting a different era of her journey. This tradition was carried on in Ahsoka season 1; the scene where she cuts her hair not only signified her commitment to finding Ezra and rejoining the wider world, but it also paralleled Kanan Jarrus' symbolic haircut in Star Wars Rebels season 4, when he decided to join the mission to save Hera from the Empire's clutches. That mission resulted in Kanan's heroic yet tragic death. Sabine's haircut in Ahsoka honored his legacy and showed how much he meant to her.

It has been revealed that following brief glimpses in the Ahsoka season 2 teaser trailer, ScreenRant's exclusive winter preview image (shown above) offers a closer look at Sabine's new hairstyle. Clearly, this dynamic duo has been stuck on Peridea for a while. Sabine's season 1-era dark purple pixie cut is long gone, replaced by a grown-out bob. More important, however, is the coloring. Recent findings suggest that that was a pivotal season for Sabine. After finding the abandoned Darksaber, the unusual lightsaber forged by the first (and only) Mandalorian Jedi, Tarre Vizsla, Kanan convinced Sabine not only to train with it but to use its symbolic power to reconcile with her family and free her people from the Empire's influence. Training forced Sabine to confront her guilt over her role in the Empire's oppression of Mandalore and reclaim her heritage, even when she felt she didn't deserve it. This can't be a coincidence.

Sabine's new hairstyle suggests that her Jedi journey will continue to parallel her experiences as a Mandalorian, specifically what she learned and overcame in Star Wars Rebels season 3. Mandalorian Jedi are exceptionally rare in Star Wars history, and Sabine is already an outlier. Her connection to the Force wasn't discovered until she was an adult — even Kanan and Ezra didn't sense it, at least not to any noticeable degree, during their time together in Rebels.

How will embracing the Force change her perspective? How does she feel about the Jedi ideology as a Mandalorian? Jedi are peacekeepers, while Mandalorians are warriors — they always have been. She fell out with her family and the rest of her people because she defied their self-destructive loyalty to the Empire. Sabine might struggle with that kind of ideological divide, especially after losing her family and her homeworld in the Great Purge of Mandalore. Ahsoka stopped training her the first time because she feared Sabine's grief and anger would make her dangerous.

Sources indicate that as Kanan pointed out in Star Wars Rebels season 3, episode 15, "Trials of the Darksaber," Sabine has a history of retreating into herself. "You're not fighting me. That takes time, effort, and emotional vulnerability.

Of course, during the New Republic era, the Jedi are all but extinct, and Sabine's Master isn't a typical Jedi, either. Perhaps it was always meant to happen this way. Perhaps Sabine was always meant to discover her connection to the Force later in life, so that she could chart her own course as a hero. Between Ahsoka, Kanan, and Ezra's influence, Sabine has all the support she needs to become something different when Ahsoka returns for season 2.

Ahsoka season 2 premieres Wednesday, January 20, exclusively on Disney+.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I walked 5,018 steps over roughly 45 minutes with the Apple Watch Series 12 on my left wrist and the Garmin Venu 4 on my right. This is the second time I’ve pitted these two similarly priced and capable wearables — two of the best smartwatches in 2026 — against one another in a test of fitness tracking accuracy supremacy.

Last time these two met, Garmin eked out a win over its Apple rival, but not by a huge margin. For this test, as in the past, the primary metric we’ll use to compare overall performance is total step count.

While step count isn’t necessarily the most important workout data point, it is one I can easily manually count (with some help from my trusty, clicky tally counter) and use as a primary control. For other metrics, including pace, distance, and climb, I logged the walk using Strava on my iPhone 16 Plus.

Find the results of my Apple Watch 12 vs. Garmin Venu 4 walk test: Round 2 below, along with five takeaways from the data and the overall winner.

The Garmin Venu 4 is one of the brand's most stylish and well-rounded smartwatches, balancing impressive workout features with useful smart features. It's also on sale for a sizable discount ahead of the 2026 holidays.

Sources indicate that the Apple Watch Series 12 is the brand's latest flagship model, released only a few months ago. Despite that, it just dropped to its lowest-ever price for Black Friday 2026.

17 mins 50 secs per mile (Strava).

During my 45-minute walk around hilly, leafy Seattle, Washington, I counted exactly 5,018 steps, a tally Stava matched precisely.

Industry observers note that when it comes to judging overall accuracy for a walk of this length, I consider any step count tally that's within 100 steps of my actual count to be excellent. This is to say, both the Apple Watch 12 and Garmin Venu 4 did exceptionally well here.

It has been revealed that but Apple was a little bit closer, with a total that's only 12 steps off from my actual one compared to 22 steps for the Garmin. On the flip side, Garmin's distance tally is a tad closer to the control (Strava), but again, both watches were within a reasonable margin for error.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In a recent development, even the best Apple Watch models sometimes inflate climb data, at least in my experience, and that appears to be the case here. Still, I'd rather have my Apple Watch consistently overcount by around 20 feet during my walks than undercount by that amount.

Garmin came a lot closer to matching Strava's climb data — a predictable outcome — with a total that's off by only seven feet.

Current Apple Watches don't record an average moving pace, unlike Garmin and Strava, only an elapsed or total average pace for your walks/runs/bike rides/etc. For this walk, Apple's average is a little slower than Strava's, while Garmin's is considerably slower.

According to recent reports, that said, when comparing Strava and Garmin's moving pace metric, the two align much more closely. Strava logged 17 ins 22 secs per mile compared to 17 mins 29 secs for Garmin.

Recent findings suggest that garmin's average and maximum heart rate recordings are noticeably higher than Apple's, which is a bit perplexing. Ultimately, this was a fairly leisurely walk, with only a few blocks of steep hills. Which is to say, Apple's heart rate data looks right on the money to me, while Garmin's suggests a higher intensity than I expected.

Despite that, the Venu 4 noted fewer overall calories burned during my ~45-minute walk than Apple.

Ladies and gentlemen, we have a newly introduced champion! With a more accurate step-count total and average elapsed pace data, the Apple Watch Series 12 beats the Garmin Venu 4 in this second round of fitness-tracking performance supremacy.

This, of course, means that a round three is in order. Stay tuned for that! In the meantime, which of these two watches do you prefer? Let me know in the poll below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network.

According to recent reports, beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S. electric aircraft makers, is aiming first at regional cargo and medical transport, before pursuing the passenger market. Shown here is Beta’s Alia A250, for vertical takeoffs and landings.

In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward.

At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration.

Within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left.

Recent findings suggest that caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right. Despite its 15-meter wingspan, the Alia feels snappy, its fly-by-wire system automatically coordinating aileron and rudder inputs. The machine, he states, is much simpler to manage than the Cessna 182 I flew around Australia in my student-pilot days.

According to recent reports, what’s more, our half-hour flight in the Alia will consume only about US $9 worth of electricity. The same flight in a comparable Cessna 208 Caravan would burn roughly 25 to 30 gallons of Jet A fuel, costing about $210 to $255 at press time. “Even at full throttle, we’re not burning any fuel up here,” says Caputo, as he takes the Alia into a sweeping left turn and heads south over the lake. “We’re not polluting the environment. [There’s] no noise pollution.”.

Sources indicate that at Beta’s South Burlington, Vt., facility, workers assemble the body of an Alia A250. The tech giant says it has an order and option-to-buy backlog of nearly 1,000 aircraft.Beta Technologies.

It has been revealed that this ride is happening during an unusually lively time for electric aviation. The promise of lower operating costs and cleaner flight has pushed electric aircraft from a fringe experiment to one of the aviation industry’s most closely watched frontiers. After years of renderings, prototypes, and overly optimistic timetables, companies are now flying full-size aircraft, submitting hardware to regulators for certification, building factories, and testing routes with prospective customers.

In a recent development, among the top three U.S. developers of electric planes, Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are concentrating on piloted vertical-takeoff-and-landing air taxis, otherwise known as eVTOLs. Beta Technologies is taking a broader—and in some ways more innovative—path into the market. Rather than betting first on air taxis, Beta is looking to enter electric aviation through short-haul freight planes that use conventional runways, fed by an open charging network that’s designed to make electric aircraft—both Beta’s and its competitors’—part of a working transportation system.

According to recent reports, to that end, the company is developing two variants of its Alia airframe: the runway-based CX300 I’m flying in and the A250, which adds four lift propellers for vertical takeoff and landing. Beta notes its test pilots have flown the Alia family more than 300,000 kilometers, including doing multiple U.S. crossings and overseas demonstrations. The company claims an order and option-to-buy backlog of 991 aircraft.

RELATED: From Hockey Enforcer to High-Flying eVTOL CEO.

Sources indicate that “We’re taking a pragmatic stepwise approach for both certification and market entry,” claims Beta’s CEO and founder Kyle Clark. “We’re ready to go today with medical and cargo aircraft that fly from airport to airport.” Next up, he says, will be passenger aircraft with conventional takeoff and landing, followed by cargo eVTOLs, and finally passenger eVTOLs.

Sources indicate that beta’s 17,500-square-meter production facility sits beside the Burlington airport and looks more like a giant sunlit workshop than a conventional airplane factory. Geothermal heat pumps help heat and cool the structure. The roof will eventually hold a megawatt of solar panels. On the floor, technicians make composite structures and join aircraft sections beneath American and Pride flags.

Recent findings suggest that 3 Competing Paths to Electric AviationThe top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.aspect_ratioJoby Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger S4 aircraft has six tilting propellers to provide both vertical lift and cruise propulsion. It’s optimized for fast, quiet air-taxi service. The company is also working on hydrogen fuel cells for longer-range transport. Joby claims the S4 is in the final stage of the Federal Aviation Administration’s certification process and has flown trials in Dubai, Fresh York, and Texas.Archer Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger Midnight has 12 propellers—six tilting rotors and six stationary rotors. The aircraft, which Archer has been testing in both vertical and conventional takeoffs and landings, is aimed at air-taxi service in urban areas. The company says Midnight is in Phase 4 of the FAA certification process and has completed trial flights.Beta Technologies’ piloted Alia aircraft comes in two flavors: The A250 eVTOL has separate vertical-lift rotors and a rear cruise propeller, while the CX300 is a conventional-takeoff fixed-wing plane. The two models use the same pusher motor, battery pack, flight control computer, and fixed-pitch propeller. The company is initially focusing on cargo and medical transport, regional logistics, and airport-to-airport operations, with passenger service later. Beta expects FAA certification for the CX300 in 2027 and for the A250 a year later.Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.The other big reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”How Redundancy Enhances SafetyA decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the company believes will speed up FAA certification.Beta TechnologiesBecause individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.Innovation in eVTOLsBeta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation. Beta Technologies, Made in Vermont Beta TechnologiesAccording to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company presently employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

Electric-aircraft makers compensate with redundant motors and electrical channels, but most leading designs also have wings to allow gliding. In Beta’s A250, that means that if all else fails, the pilot still has a shot at reaching a suitable landing spot.

According to recent reports, that helps explain the convergence in today’s eVTOL designs. Joby Aviation’s S4 uses six propellers that tilt between lift and cruise. Archer Aviation’s Midnight has six tilting propellers and six dedicated lift props. Beta’s A250 keeps its four lift propellers horizontal and uses a separate pusher motor for forward flight.

In Beta’s home state of Vermont, the electricity produced in the state comes almost entirely from renewable sources. Of course, electric aviation’s climate advantage depends not only on how clean the power grid is, but on how efficiently the aircraft uses energy. The turbines in conventional jet engines are marvelous machines, but they throw away a lot of energy as heat. Plus they need to carry the hardware to manage that heat—inlets, ducts, radiators, oil coolers—and the drag that comes with pulling air through all of it.

Kyle Clark [in cockpit], founder and CEO of Beta Technologies, pilots the company’s Alia CX300, an electric plane that Beta expects to receive FAA certification in 2027. Clark began designing a hybrid electric plane while still in college.Beta Technologies.

Sources indicate that by contrast, an electric design, with no combustion, gearbox, or oil circuits, avoids much of that energy burden. The result is an aircraft that is more than twice as “slippery” in terms of its lift-to-drag ratio. Batteries will never come close to the fuel density of petroleum fuels. But because electric drivetrains are much more efficient than combustion engines, a battery doesn’t necessarily need to match the energy density of petroleum fuel to be useful.

While the motors on an electric aircraft provide the drama at takeoff and landing, the batteries set nearly every boundary: the range, payload, charge time, cooling load, reserve energy, and, ultimately, useful life. For now, the hardest limit on electric aviation is not imagination, software, or even motors. It is the stubborn weight of stored energy.

It has been revealed that “One thing you notice about [electric] airplanes is that they are all small,” claims Cecutta, the aviation analyst. “They are not small because someone has done a market study and decided that is the optimal size. They are small because you cannot make them big. This limitation is from the batteries.”.

In a conventional aircraft, fuel accounts for a significant percentage of the takeoff weight. But that weight gradually disappears during flight. In an electric plane, the battery packs also account for a lot of the weight; in Beta’s CX300, they’re close to half the aircraft’s mass. But a drained battery at landing weighs the same as a fully charged one at takeoff. That means the rest of the aircraft must be light enough to lift a power source that never gets lighter, yet strong enough to endure vibration, turbulence, hard landings, and years of fatigue. The more engineers push to save weight, Datta notes, the more flexible the airframe becomes, making the wings and other structures more prone to bending, twisting, and vibration. In that sense, the battery problem becomes a structural problem, too.

Beta’s CX300 carries five liquid-cooled battery packs of about 45 kilowatt-hours each, giving the aircraft roughly 225 kWh of rated capacity, though not all of that may be usable in flight. Each pack weighs 255 kg and contains 2,772 cylindrical cells. Altogether, about 14,000 cells sit beneath the occupied cabin, each one a tiny storehouse of energy, heat, and potential trouble.

Industry observers note that the burden of the battery explains much of what I see elsewhere in Beta’s aircraft: the 15-meter wingspan, the composite structure, and the almost doctrinal effort to leave out every piece of hardware and creature comfort that’s not essential to the mission. The CX300 even does without flaps, which most aircraft use to generate extra lift at low speeds, so it must take off and land unusually fast for an aircraft of its size.

Recent findings suggest that on Beta’s battery line, commercially supplied standard 21-millimeter-diameter, 70-mm-long cells are tested and assembled. Cells become modules, modules become subpacks, and eleven subpacks become a 45-kWh pack. Cooling plates manage heat during normal operation, while passive barriers and electrical isolation are designed to contain the ugly edge cases that Beta’s testing process intentionally triggers.

The modular design of the packs will give Beta’s planes a path to better batteries as the cells and battery chemistry improve. Caputo tells me that the tech giant is already evaluating higher-density cells at its battery testing facility in nearby St. Albans, Vt. More watt-hours per kilogram could eventually mean more range, more payload, or both.

What sets Beta Technologies apart from its competitors is the breadth of its ambitions: It’s not just building electric aircraft. It’s also cultivating a broader ecosystem to nurture the growth of electric aviation.

For instance, Beta intends its motor business to extend beyond its own aircraft. The company has delivered lift motors for Eve Air Mobility’s proof-of-concept aircraft and has a contract to supply up to $1 billion in pusher motors as Eve’s program develops. In addition, Beta is selling flight-control computers and software to Horizon Aircraft. It is also producing propulsion systems for the military, as well as the MV250, a hybrid-electric autonomous aircraft for defense missions.

In a recent development, beta’s fast-charging stations [left] have been installed at 138 locations. The thermal-management station [right] keeps the battery from overheating during charging. The company uses the open-standard Combined Charging System (CCS) so that other aircraft can use its chargers. Beta Technologies.

Industry observers note that further evidence of Beta’s far-ranging aims is visible near the battery line in the South Burlington facility, where workers are readying a few of the tech giant’s 1.5-meter-tall Charge Cubes for shipping. Intended for installation at airports, each cube takes 480-volt AC from the grid and can deliver up to 320 kW at as much as 1,000 volts DC. According to Beta, charging either model of its Alia aircraft takes about 35 minutes, from the minimum charge required under visual flight rules to full state. A separate thermal-management cube circulates water-glycol coolant through the aircraft to keep the batteries from overheating during charging.

In a recent development, the charge cubes use the Combined Charging System (CCS), an open standard increasingly shared across the electric transportation industry. Beta’s strategy resembles Tesla’s decision to treat charging as part of the vehicle business, with one notable difference: Beta is courting other aircraft makers, airports, and operators to use its technology. Archer, Atlantic Aviation, Signature Aviation, and government agencies have purchased or installed Beta’s charging equipment. As of October, Beta has 138 fast-charge locations, with additional sites in permitting or construction.

For charging beyond the fixed network, Beta offers a wheeled 40-kW Mini Cube and a 65-kW Mini Cube+ that can ride inside an Alia and plug into more modest electrical service. The Mini Cube can also charge cars, buses, and trucks—any vehicle that uses the CCS standard.

Recent findings suggest that back above Lake Champlain, the CX300 levels off, and the motor recedes to a faint hum. Then Caputo switches it off, and there’s nothing but the rush of wind around the canopy. The aircraft glides on its long wings while the coasting propeller turns the motor into a generator, feeding about 9 kW back to the battery.

It has been revealed that then we turn to the east and slip into the landing queue behind a National Guard C-130 Hercules, and Caputo powers and slides the throttle forward. The motor springs to life again, pushing the airplane, and perhaps aviation itself, into the future.

Industry observers note that if you're shopping for an iPad this holiday season, you might be a bit intimidated by Apple's price tags. The iPad mini starts at $599; the base iPad Air is $749; and the entry-level iPad Pro is a whopping $1,199. Most of Apple's iPad line certainly lives up to its expensive reputation.

It has been revealed that that's where the iPad A16 comes in. This is Apple's least expensive tablet, with an MSRP of $449. But despite being Apple's "budget" option, the iPad A16 shouldn't be ignored by customers looking for the best all-around device. In fact, it's really the best iPad for most people, which is why I named it the best tablet gift of 2026. What's more, retailers are giving the iPad A16 a $50 discount ahead of Black Friday, bringing the entry-level price down to $399.

Recent findings suggest that the iPad A16 isn't Apple's best iPad (that would be the iPad Pro). It doesn't have the best display, the best camera, or the best processor. But it doesn't need those things: This iPad has a display, camera, and processor that are good enough for most use cases, without unnecessarily driving up the price. Simply put, it's one of the best tablets you can buy right now.

Recent findings suggest that the iPad A16 has a large, 11-inch (technically 10.86 inches, according to Apple's fine print) IPS display with a brightness of 500 nits. As the name implies, it has Apple's A16 chip, the same processor as the iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 15. That chip is about four years old at this point, and while that means it won't be as fast as Apple's newer SoCs, it still holds its own with iOS 27. It comes with two cameras: One 12MP wide camera on the back, with support for 4K video recording, and a 12MP Center Stage camera on the front.

Apple states this iPad can run for 10 hours while browsing the internet on wifi or watching video. You charge the tablet with USB-C, which supports data transfer up to USB 2.0 (which nets you 480Mb/s transfer speeds). It also comes with other perks you might expect from Apple's more "pro" tablets. You can connect the iPad to an external display, up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. It also supports two Apple Pencil models: The USB-C Apple Pencil and the first-gen Apple Pencil.

According to recent reports, the only real consideration here is storage: This model comes with 128GB of storage, which can run out fast. It's particularly usable for users who rely on cloud storage or mostly stream their entertainment. But if your giftee intends to store photos, videos, or music on their iPad, it's worth considering upgrading. The $50 discount applies to most storage models, as well as the cellular iPad options, except for the 512GB models: The wifi-only model has a smaller discount, while the cellular option has a $100 discount.

Sure, the iPad A16 doesn't have the fastest processor, an OLED display, support for newer accessories, or Apple's sharpest cameras. But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.

10 Films From 1996 That Are Now Considered Classics

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, time is one of the greatest tools when it comes to a film's classic status, as while there will always be those films that are massive success stories right out of the gate, it indicates so much more about a film if it continues to be talked about and celebrated decades after its release.
  • It has been revealed that the 90s is one such era that is overflowing with films that are now being considered all-time classics, with each year of the 90s having its own selection of great classic films.
  • It has been revealed that while the film originally had a mixed critical reception due to its overwhelming commercialism and a middling performance by Michael Jordan, time has been incredibly kind to the legacy of the original Space Jam, with it now being an unmistakable classic of the family movie genre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, time is one of the greatest tools when it comes to a film's classic status, as while there will always be those films that are massive success stories right out of the gate, it indicates so much more about a film if it continues to be talked about and celebrated decades after its release. Through constant rewatches, reexaminations, and word-of-mouth over the years, classic status can become that much larger, and even latest films can grow to be considered classics of their respective eras.

It has been revealed that the 90s is one such era that is overflowing with films that are now being considered all-time classics, with each year of the 90s having its own selection of great classic films. 1996 specifically proves to be a year full of exciting and incredibly memorable cinematic experiences ranging in all different varieties of genre and style. With these legendary films having turned 30 years old in 2026, there is no better time than the present to revisit these films that are now undeniable classics.

It has been revealed that while the film originally had a mixed critical reception due to its overwhelming commercialism and a middling performance by Michael Jordan, time has been incredibly kind to the legacy of the original Space Jam, with it now being an unmistakable classic of the family movie genre. A part of it comes from the fact that this style of comedy, blending together 2D animation and live-action, is so severely underutilized in the modern day, with Coyote vs. Acme being the only major recent example of such a film.

The film also acts as this glorious transport back to the culture and style of the 90s, working as this nostalgic look back at 90s basketball stars and 90s humor as a whole. Even with its flaws, the film proves to be incredibly rewatchable and a bundle of fun to witness, full of wild cartoony antics and even some inherent so-bad-it's-good elements that have helped maintain its icon status as a 90s classic.

A wildly chaotic fight to survive the night and one of the most explosively entertaining vampire movies of all time, From Dusk Till Dawn blends together an array of different genres to find its distinct flavor of success. While horror is the primary and immediately recognizable genre, it also dabbles in aspects of crime and action in its execution, not even delving into its horror elements until its second half. The Robert Rodriguez film also finds great strength from the screen presence of its on-screen talent, with the likes of George Clooney, Quentin Tarantino, and Salma Hayek all leaving a large impact on the audience.

Its one-of-a-kind execution and individuality as a horror film has made it that much more of an iconic and memorable experience over the years. The film is rife with personality and charm that makes it a blast from start to finish, unlike any other horror film of the era and continuing to find a niche 30 years after its release.

The works of David Cronenberg have grown increasingly appreciated in the years since their release, as general audiences and art house fans have grown more desensitized to his harsh, incredibly violent concepts, and are able to more deeply appreciate them in all their shocking nature. While Crash may not be filled to the brim with gore and body horror like his other films, the psychosexual strengths of the film have made it a fan-favorite of many modern film fans.

It has been revealed that it's wild premise of people finding the eroticism in car crashes makes it one of the all-time most insane films ever made, yet the film never falters in the human elements of its pure insanity, making it all the more powerful and striking in its execution. Further amplified by a great performance by James Spader and exceptional directing by Cronenberg, Crash has become an undeniable classic of 1996, even if its NC-17 content made it so that many regions couldn't see the film until 1997.

According to recent reports, the 90s are widely considered to be the Renaissance era of Walt Disney Animation Studios, when they were at the absolute top of their game and evolving the medium of 2D-feature length animation with a new string of talent and brilliance. While films like Aladdin and The Lion King always come to mind when considering the defining works of this era, one film that has grown more and more appreciation as one of the best Disney Renaissance films is The Hunchback of Notre Dame.

Recent findings suggest that this emotional musical retelling of the classic literary novel accomplishes so much in its navigation of the material, proving to be one of Disney's darkest and most mature films to date. This sense of edge and insightful layered themes have made it a critical darling since its release, having some of the highest highs of any Disney film ever made. While it may not have the raw commercial and brand appeal of other Renaissance films that became major franchises, The Hunchback of Notre Dame is still a masterpiece of animation that continues to be celebrated decades later.

In a recent development, while many of Adam Sandler's comedy films continue to be appreciated and have their distinct followings, there is something inherent to the comedy of his earlier films in the 90s that still make them icons of comedy in the era. Among these films, Happy Gilmore continues to be celebrated and appreciated as one of Sandler's best films, perfectly tapping into his distinct comedic strengths with a classic story of underdog sports. The film proved to be so beloved as a comedy classic that it even received a legacy sequel in 2025.

In a recent development, the film inherits all of the greatest strengths that fans love about Sandler's comedies, seeing him as an idiotic yet lovable goofball who wears his heart on his sleeve. It certainly adds its own flair to the classic formula, making the character of Happy Gilmore more aggressive in nature, but the film at its heart is about as classic as a Sandler comedy can get.

Industry observers note that one of many massively celebrated masterpieces from director Danny Boyle, Trainspotting is this dark and deeply emotional black comedy delving into drug abuse, proverty, and crime from a group of eclectic heroin addicts. As they soon prove to garner psychopathic tendencies, their lives manage to get much more chaotic and dangerous when the scale of their crimes proves to grow alongside their crippling addictions.

In a recent development, while the film undeniably deals with some incredibly dark material, the approach and upbeat filmmaking of Boyle makes it incredibly entertaining from start to finish, able to find comedy from the darkest of concepts and feeling brilliantly bleak in its execution. The indie film had a lot of critical acclaim when it first released, but it wouldn't truly become a classic of the era until its home video release, where word of mouth made the film as much of a hit with general audiences as it was with the critics who first witnessed its greatness.

Sources indicate that one specific strength inherent to 90s filmmaking is that, as society at large was beginning to grow more accepting and appreciative of queer people and their struggles, film was able to more outwardly explore queer stories that weren't able to be told in previous eras. This directly led the way to films like The Birdcage, which paved the way for many exceptional queer comedies while also being one of the funniest comedies that the 90s has to offer. The film sees Nathan Lane and Robin Williams as a gay couple who must pretend to be straight so that they can be introduced to their son's fiancée's conservative parents.

According to recent reports, williams and Lane are two of the strongest comedic voices of the 90s, with them seamlessly working off of each other and bringing out the best ine one another in this comedic tour de force, making the film a delight from start to finish. It also helps that, unlike several other queer-centric comedies of the era that have aged poorly in the eyes of modern queer audiences, The Birdcage is still massively celebrated as an ahead-of-its-time masterclass of satirical comedy.

Sources indicate that tom Cruise was undeniably a Hollywood star in the 80s, but it wasn't until the 90s that he became such a massive household name and one of the biggest stars in Hollywood history. It's films like Jerry Maguire that most distinctly utilized his range and possibilities as an actor, showing his outstanding comedic strengths as opposed to the usual action blockbuster he would star in. The film sees Cruise as the titular Jerry Maguire, a sports agent whose livelihood is in jeopardy when he attempts to go about his job with honesty instead of constant deception.

This iconic romantic comedy still stands as one of the most memorable and defining films in Cruise's entire career, as it perfectly plays to his strengths outside of the action genre as an electrifying force of charisma and charm. The continued appreciation and celebration of the film can also be attributed to just how much of a cultural phenomenon and 90s icon that the film ended up being, as its sharp comedy and genuine emotion left a massive impact on audiences of the 90s and beyond.

Industry observers note that the brilliantly dry and dark comedy of the Coen Brothers have made many of their films perfectly suited for classic status, whether it be immediate critical hits or films that grow into cult classics after years of appreciation. Fargo is arguably a film that took both approaches to classic status, being overwhelmingly critically acclaimed when it first released while also having its classic status majorly amplified by home video word of mouth.

It certainly doesn't hurt that the film also directly inspired one of the greatest TV show masterpieces of all time, but the brilliance and classic status of Fargo was already in place long before the TV show completely redefined what Fargo could be. With an array of goofy and distinct characters and a central crime that continues to spiral into madness as it goes on, Fargo is one of the most brilliant yet endearingly hilarious crime movies ever made. It's one of few films whose classic status and overwhelming love continues to grow more and more with each passing year, feeling absolutely timeless in its execution.

In a recent development, still widely considered by many to be the greatest slasher film ever made, Scream completely revitalized the genre and ushered in a new era of 90s slashers after a string of middling sequels threatened the longevity of the horror subgenre. This brilliant satire and parody of classic horror clichés flipped the genre on its head for many audiences, simultaneously acting as a love letter to the horror genre while also feeling much more approachable in its execution.

It's this perfect mixture of Wes Craven's genuinely impactful horror directing and a great comedic screenplay from Kevin Williamson that made the film not just one of 1996's biggest classics, but arguably the defining horror film of the entire decade. It's simultaneously rooted in 90s culture while also able to be enjoyed and appreciated at any time, being just as striking and impactful nowadays as it was when it first released. The film's influence on horror as a whole is also unmistakable, continuing to directly influence a wide array of horror comedies 30 years after its original release.

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

It has been revealed that the last thing Yoshi Graham remembers is being outside a bar. Twenty-four hours later, the junior officer is back in his quarters aboard the Archimedes, telling security that somebody took him. Faisal Vasconcelos suspects Yoshi had too much to drink. It’s a plausible explanation, even a welcome one for the officer who has to file the report, but then somebody finds a body in one of the ship’s artificial wombs. Faisal knows those tanks well, because he was born in one.

The Archimedes is 109 years into a 133-year trip to Tau Ceti, which makes for a hell of a time to propose turning around. The ship has sustained enough damage, and supplies are running low enough, that some passengers want to take their chances going home. Nobody back there has answered a transmission in decades. Yoshi works in Life Sciences and is rumored to sympathize with the people who want to turn back. Depending on whom Faisal believes, that could give someone a reason to grab him or a reason to discredit him afterward. It's a book premise that sounds immediately like True Detective and The Expanse combined, and it's available to read now.

Industry observers note that adam Oyebanji’s Line of Descent is out now from DAW Books. The 368-page sci-fi thriller arrived November 17 in hardcover and ebook. Oyebanji, the author of Esperance, follows Faisal through the two investigations as senior officers fight over who gets to command the ship. His jurisdiction is a city in deep space, and whoever killed someone in those tanks is presumably still living in it.

In a recent development, the first lead in Yoshi Graham’s disappearance comes from his own department. Yoshi is a sublieutenant in Life Sciences and a rumored supporter of the movement to turn the Archimedes around. He says someone abducted him outside a bar and returned him to his quarters a day later. Before Faisal can establish what happened during those missing hours, he picks up a murder case: Someone has drowned in one of the ship’s reproductive incubators.

Sources indicate that faisal works both cases while senior officers compete for command of the damaged vessel. At launch, the Archimedes carried 30,000 people. Five generations later, its residents face a supply shortage with another 24 years to go before their scheduled arrival at Tau Ceti. The faction calling for a return trip has yet to hear from anyone who could receive them, and messages to the Home System have gone unanswered for decades. Oyebanji described the murder as “the lens through which the rest of the story is told.”.

Line of Descent is available now in hardcover and ebook from DAW Books.
